1.17: OF INDUCTIVE AND DYNAMIC PSYCHOLOGY EDITOR'S INTRODUCTION The present volume appeals to the editor of this series as one of the
1.18: most significant books, viewed from the standpoint of the future of our educational theory and practice, that has been issued in
1.19: years. Not only does the volume set forth, in language so simple that the layman can easily understand, the large importance fo
1.20: r public education of a careful measurement of the intelligence of children, but it also describes the tests which are to be giv
1.21: en and the entire procedure of giving them. In a clear and easy style the author sets forth scientific facts of farreaching educ
1.22: ational importance, facts which it has cost him, his students, and many other scientific workers, years of painstaking labor to
1.23: accumulate. Only very recently, practically only within the past halfdozen years, have scientific workers begun to appreciate fu
1.24: lly the importance of intelligence tests as a guide to educational procedure, and up to the present we have been able to make bu
1.25: t little use of such tests in our schools. The conception in itself has been new, and the testing procedure has been more or les
1.26: s unrefined and technical. The following somewhat popular presentation of the idea and of the methods involved, itself based on
1.27: a scientific monograph which the author is publishing elsewhere, serves for the first time to set forth in simple language the t
1.28: echnical details of giving such intelligence tests. The educational significance of the results to be obtained from careful meas
1.29: urements of the intelligence of children can hardly be overestimated. Questions relating to the choice of studies, vocational gu
1.30: idance, schoolroom procedure, the grading of pupils, promotional schemes, the study of the retardation of children in the school
1.31: s, juvenile delinquency, and the proper handling of subnormals on the one hand and gifted children on the other,all alike acquir
1.32: e new meaning and significance when viewed in the light of the measurement of intelligence as outlined in this volume. As a guid
1.33: e to the interpretation of the results of other forms of investigation relating to the work, progress, and needs of children, in
1.34: telligence tests form a very valuable aid. More than all other forms of data combined, such tests give the necessary information
1.35: from which a pupil's possibilities of future mental growth can be foretold, and upon which his further education can be most pr
1.36: ofitably directed. The publication of this revision and extension of the original BinetSimon scale for measuring intelligence, w
1.37: ith the closer adaptation of it to American conditions and needs, should mark a distinct step in advance in our educational proc
1.38: edure. It means the perfection of another and a very important measuring stick for evaluating educational practices, and in part
1.39: icular for diagnosing individual possibilities and needs. Just now the method is new, and its use somewhat limited, but it is th
1.40: e confident prediction of many students of the subject that, before long, intelligence tests will become as much a matter of nec
1.41: essary routine in schoolroom procedure as a bloodcount now is in physical diagnosis. That our schoolroom methods will in turn be
1.42: come much more intelligent, and that all classes of children, but especially the gifted and the slow, will profit by such intell
1.43: ectual diagnosis, there can be but little question. That any parent or teacher, without training, can give these tests, the auth
1.44: or in no way contends. However, the observations of Dr. Kohs, cited in Chapter VII, as well as the experience of the author and
1.45: others who have given courses in intelligence testing to teachers, alike indicate that sufficient skill to enable teachers and s

3.37: 279 THE MEASUREMENT OF INTELLIGENCE PART I PROBLEMS AND RESULTS THE MEASUREMENT OF INTELLIGENCE CHAPTER I THE USES OF
3.38: INTELLIGENCE TESTS INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF RETARDED SCHOOL CHILDREN. Numerous studies of the agegrade progress of school children
3.39: have afforded convincing evidence of the magnitude and seriousness of the retardation problem. Statistics collected in hundreds
3.40: of cities in the United States show that between a third and a half of the school children fail to progress through the grades
3.41: at the expected rate; that from 10 to 15 per cent are retarded two years or more; and that from 5 to 8 per cent are retarded at
3.42: least three years. More than 10 per cent of the $400,000,000 annually expended in the United States for school instruction is de
3.43: voted to reteaching children what they have already been taught but have failed to learn. The first efforts at reform which resu
3.44: lted from these findings were based on the supposition that the evils which had been discovered could be remedied by the individ
3.45: ualizing of instruction, by improved methods of promotion, by increased attention to children's health, and by other reforms in
3.46: school administration. Although reforms along these lines have been productive of much good, they have nevertheless been in a me
3.47: asure disappointing. The trouble was, they were too often based upon the assumption that under the right conditions all children
3.48: would be equally, or almost equally, capable of making satisfactory school progress. Psychological studies of school children b
3.49: y means of standardized intelligence tests have shown that this supposition is not in accord with the facts. It has been found t
3.50: hat children do not fall into two welldefined groups, the "feebleminded" and the "normal." Instead, there are many grades of int
3.51: elligence, ranging from idiocy on the one hand to genius on the other. Among those classed as normal, vast individual difference
3.52: s have been found to exist in original mental endowment, differences which affect profoundly the capacity to profit from school
3.53: instruction. We are beginning to realize that the school must take into account, more seriously than it has yet done, the existe
3.54: nce and significance of these differences in endowment. Instead of wasting energy in the vain attempt to hold mentally slow and
3.55: defective children up to a level of progress which is normal to the average child, it will be wiser to take account of the inequ
3.56: alities of children in original endowment and to differentiate the course of study in such a way that each child will be allowed
3.57: to progress at the rate which is normal to him, whether that rate be rapid or slow. While we cannot hold all children to the sa
3.58: me standard of school progress, we can at least prevent the kind of retardation which involves failure and the repetition of a s
3.59: chool grade. It is well enough recognized that children do not enter with very much zest upon school work in which they have onc
3.60: e failed. Failure crushes selfconfidence and destroys the spirit of work. It is a sad fact that a large proportion of children i
3.61: n the schools are acquiring the habit of failure. The remedy, of course, is to measure out the work for each child in proportion
3.62: to his mental ability. Before an engineer constructs a railroad bridge or trestle, he studies the materials to be used, and lea
3.63: rns by means of tests exactly the amount of strain per unit of size his materials will be able to withstand. He does not work em
3.64: pirically, and count upon patching up the mistakes which may later appear under the stress of actual use. The educational engine

4.1: er should emulate this example. Tests and forethought must take the place of failure and patchwork. Our efforts have been too lo
4.2: ng directed by "trial and error." It is time to leave off guessing and to acquire a scientific knowledge of the material with wh
4.3: ich we have to deal. When instruction must be repeated, it means that the school, as well as the pupil, has failed. Every child
4.4: who fails in his school work or is in danger of failing should be given a mental examination. The examination takes less than on
4.5: e hour, and the result will contribute more to a real understanding of the case than anything else that could be done. It is nec
4.6: essary to determine whether a given child is unsuccessful in school because of poor native ability, or because of poor instructi
4.7: on, lack of interest, or some other removable cause. It is not sufficient to establish any number of special classes, if they ar
4.8: e to be made the dumpingground for all kinds of troublesome casesthe feebleminded, the physically defective, the merely backward
4.9: , the truants, the incorrigibles, etc. Without scientific diagnosis and classification of these children the educational work of
4.10: the special class must blunder along in the dark. In such diagnosis and classification our main reliance must always be in ment
4.11: al tests, properly used and properly interpreted. INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF THE FEEBLEMINDED. Thus far intelligence tests have found
4.12: their chief application in the identification and grading of the feebleminded. Their value for this purpose is twofold. In the
4.13: first place, it is necessary to ascertain the degree of defect before it is possible to decide intelligently upon either the con
4.14: tent or the method of instruction suited to the training of the backward child. In the second place, intelligence tests are rapi
4.15: dly extending our conception of "feeblemindedness" to include milder degrees of defect than have generally been associated with
4.16: this term. The earlier methods of diagnosis caused a majority of the higher grade defectives to be overlooked. Previous to the d
4.17: evelopment of psychological methods the lowgrade moron was about as high a type of defective as most physicians or even psycholo
4.18: gists were able to identify as feebleminded. Wherever intelligence tests have been made in any considerable number in the school
4.19: s, they have shown that not far from 2 per cent of the children enrolled have a grade of intelligence which, however long they l
4.20: ive, will never develop beyond the level which is normal to the average child of 11 or 12 years. The large majority of these bel
4.21: ong to the moron grade; that is, their mental development will stop somewhere between the 7year and 12year level of intelligence
4.22: , more often between 9 and 12. The more we learn about such children, the clearer it becomes that they must be looked upon as re
4.23: al defectives. They may be able to drag along to the fourth, fifth, or sixth grades, but even by the age of 16 or 18 years they
4.24: are never able to cope successfully with the more abstract and difficult parts of the commonschool course of study. They may mas
4.25: ter a certain amount of rote learning, such as that involved in reading and in the manipulation of number combinations but they
4.26: cannot be taught to meet new conditions effectively or to think, reason, and judge as normal persons do. It is safe to predict t
4.27: hat in the near future intelligence tests will bring tens of thousands of these highgrade defectives under the surveillance and
4.28: protection of society. This will ultimately result in curtailing the reproduction of feeblemindedness and in the elimination of
4.29: an enormous amount of crime, pauperism, and industrial inefficiency. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the highgrade case
4.30: s, of the type now so frequently overlooked, are precisely the ones whose guardianship it is most important for the State to ass
4.31: ume. INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF DELINQUENTS. One of the most important facts brought to light by the use of intelligence tests is the
4.32: frequent association of delinquency and mental deficiency. Although it has long been recognized that the proportion of feeblemi
4.33: ndedness among offenders is rather large, the real amount has, until recently, been underestimated even by the most competent st
4.34: udents of criminology. The criminologists have been accustomed to give more attention to the physical than to the mental correla
4.35: tes of crime. Thus, Lombroso and his followers subjected thousands of criminals to observation and measurement with regard to su
4.36: ch physical traits as size and shape of the skull, bilateral asymmetries, anomalies of the ear, eye, nose, palate, teeth, hands,
4.37: fingers, hair, dermal sensitivity, etc. The search was for physical "stigmata" characteristic of the "criminal type." Although
4.38: such studies performed an important service in creating a scientific interest in criminology, the theories of Lombroso have been
4.39: wholly discredited by the results of intelligence tests. Such tests have demonstrated, beyond any possibility of doubt, that th
4.40: e most important trait of at least 25 per cent of our criminals is mental weakness. The physical abnormalities which have been f
4.41: ound so common among prisoners are not the stigmata of criminality, but the physical accompaniments of feeblemindedness. They ha
4.42: ve no diagnostic significance except in so far as they are indications of mental deficiency. Without exception, every study whic
4.43: h has been made of the intelligence level of delinquents has furnished convincing testimony as to the close relation existing be
4.44: tween mental weakness and moral abnormality. Some of these findings are as follows: Miss Renz tested 100 girls of the Ohio State
4.45: Reformatory and reported 36 per cent as certainly feebleminded. In every one of these cases the commitment papers had given the

4.48: another of 15½ had 8year intelligence. Of 56 delinquent girls 14 to 20 years of age tested by Hill and Goddard, almost half belo

9.30: ] Aroused by the skepticism so often shown toward his test method, Binet decided to make a little study of the methods by which
9.31: teachers are accustomed to arrive at a judgment as to a child's intelligence. Accordingly, through the coöperation of the direct
9.32: or of elementary education in Paris, he secured answers from a number of teachers to the following questions: [8] See p. 169 _ff
9.33: ._ of reference 2, at end of this book 1. _By what means do you judge the intelligence of your pupils?_ 2. _How often have you b
9.34: een deceived in your judgments?_ About 40 replies were received. Most of the answers to the first question were vague, onesided,
9.35: "verbal," or bookish. Only a few showed much psychological discrimination as to what intelligence is and what its symptoms are.
9.36: There was a very general tendency to judge intelligence by success in one or more of the school studies. Some thought that abil
9.37: ity to master arithmetic was a sure criterion. Others were influenced almost entirely by the pupil's ability to read. One teache
9.38: r said that the child who can "read so expressively as to make you feel the punctuation" is certainly intelligent, an observatio
9.39: n which is rather good, as far as it goes. A few judged intelligence by the pupil's knowledge of such subjects as history and ge
9.40: ography, which, as Binet points out, is to confound intelligence with the ability to memorize. "Memory," says Binet, is a "great
9.41: simulator of intelligence." It is a wise teacher who is not deceived by it. Only a small minority mentioned resourcefulness in
9.42: play, capacity to adjust to practical situations, or any other outofschool criteria. Some suggested asking the pupil such questi
9.43: ons as the following: "Why do you love your parents?" "If it takes three persons seven hours to do a piece of work, would it tak
9.44: e seven persons any longer?" "Which would you rather have, a fourth of a pie, or a half of a half?" "Which is heavier, a pound o
9.45: f feathers or a pound of lead?" "If you had twenty cents what would you do with it?" A great many based their judgment mainly on
9.46: the general appearance of the face and eyes. An "active" or "passive" expression of the eyes was looked upon as especially sign
9.47: ificant. One teacher thought that a mere "glance of the eye" was sufficient to display the grade of intelligence. If the eyes ar
9.48: e penetrating, reflective, or show curiosity, the child must be intelligent; if they are heavy and expressionless, he must be du
9.49: ll. The mobility of countenance came in for frequent mention, also the shape of the head. No one will deny that intelligence dis
9.50: plays itself to a greater or less extent in the features; but how, asks Binet, are we going to _standardize_ a "glance of the ey
9.51: e" or an "expression of curiosity" so that it will serve as an exact measure of intelligence? The fact is, the more one sees of
9.52: feebleminded children, the less reliance one comes to place upon facial expression as a sign of intelligence. Some children who
9.53: are only slightly backward have the general appearance of lowgrade imbeciles. On the other hand, not a few who are distinctly fe
9.54: ebleminded are pretty and attractive. With many such children a ready smile takes the place of comprehension. If the smile is ra
9.55: ther sweet and sympathetic, as is often the case, the observer is almost sure to be deceived. As regards the shape of the head,
9.56: peculiar conformation of the ears, and other "stigmata," science long ago demonstrated that these are ordinarily of little or no
9.57: significance. In reply to the second question, some teachers stated that they never made a mistake, while others admitted failu
9.58: re in one case out of three. Still others said, "Once in ten years," "once in twenty years," "once in a thousand times," etc. As
9.59: Binet remarks, the answers to this question are not very enlightening. In the first place, the teacher as a rule loses sight of
9.60: the pupil when he has passed from her care, and seldom has opportunity of finding out whether his later success belies her judg
9.61: ment or confirms it. Errors go undiscovered for the simple reason that there is no opportunity to check them up. In the second p
9.62: lace, her estimate is so rough that an error must be very great in order to have any meaning. If I say that a man is six feet an
9.63: d two inches tall, it is easy enough to apply a measuring stick and prove the correctness or incorrectness of my assertion. But
9.64: if I say simply that the man is "rather tall," or "very tall," the error must be very extreme before we can expose it, particula

10.1: rly since the estimate can itself be checked up only by observation and not by controlled experiment. The teachers' answers seem
10.2: to justify three conclusions: 1. Teachers do not have a very definite idea of what constitutes intelligence. They tend to confu
10.3: se it variously with capacity for memorizing, facility in reading, ability to master arithmetic, etc. On the whole, their standa
10.4: rd is too academic. They fail to appreciate the onesidedness of the school's demands upon intelligence. In a quaintly humorous p
10.5: assage discussing this tendency, Binet characterizes the child in a class as _dénaturé_, a French word which we may translate (t
10.6: hough rather too literally) as "denatured." Too often this "denatured" child of the classroom is the only child the teacher know
10.7: s. 2. In judging intelligence teachers are too easily deceived by a sprightly attitude, a sympathetic expression, a glance of th
10.8: e eye, or a chance "bump" on the head. 3. Although a few teachers seem to realize the many possibilities of error, the majority
10.9: show rather undue confidence in the accuracy of their judgment. BINET'S EXPERIMENT ON HOW TEACHERS TEST INTELLIGENCE.[9] Finally
10.10: , Binet had three teachers come to his laboratory to judge the intelligence of children whom they had never seen before. Each sp
10.11: ent an afternoon in the laboratory and examined five pupils. In each case the teacher was left free to arrive at a conclusion in
10.12: her own way. Binet, who remained in the room and took notes, recounts with playful humor how the teachers were unavoidably comp
10.13: elled to resort to the muchabused test method, although their attempts at using it were sometimes, from the psychologist's point
10.14: of view, amusingly clumsy. [9] See p. 182 _ff._ of reference 2 at end of this book. One teacher, for example, questioned the ch
10.15: ildren about some canals and sluices which were in the vicinity, asking what their purpose was and how they worked. Another show
10.16: ed the children some pretty pictures, which she had brought with her for the purpose, and asked questions about them. Showing th
10.17: e picture of a garret, she asked how a garret differs from an ordinary room. One teacher asked whether in building a factory it
10.18: was best to have the walls thick or thin. As King Edward had just died, another teacher questioned the children about the detail
10.19: s of this event, in order to find out whether they were in the habit of reading the newspapers, or understood the things they he
10.20: ard others read. Other questions related to the names of the streets in the neighborhood, the road one should take to reach a ce
10.21: rtain point in the vicinity, etc. Binet notes that many of the questions were special, and were only applicable with the childre
10.22: n of this particular school. The method of proposing the questions and judging the responses was also at fault. The teachers did
10.23: not adhere consistently to any definite formula in giving a particular test to the different children. Instead, the questions w
10.24: ere materially altered from time to time. One teacher scored the identical response differently for two children, giving one chi
10.25: ld more credit than the other because she had already judged his intelligence to be superior. In several cases the examination w
10.26: as needlessly delayed in order to instruct the child in what he did not know. The examination ended, quite properly for a teache
10.27: r's examination, with questions about history, literature, the metric system, etc., and with the recitation of a fable. A compar
10.28: ison of the results showed hardly any agreement among the estimates of the three teachers. When questioned about the standard th
10.29: at had been taken in arriving at their conclusions, one teacher said she had taken the answers of the first pupil as a point of
10.30: departure, and that she had judged the other pupils by this one. Another judged all the children by a child of her acquaintance
10.31: whom she knew to be intelligent. This was, of course, an unsafe method, because no one could say how the child taken as an ideal
10.32: would have responded to the tests used with the five children. In summarizing the result of his little experiment, Binet points
10.33: out that the teachers employed, as if by instinct, the very method which he himself recommends. In using it, however, they made
10.34: numerous errors. Their questions were often needlessly long. Several were "dilemma questions," that is, answerable by _yes_ or
10.35: _no_. In such cases chance alone will cause fifty per cent of the answers to be correct. Some of the questions were merely tests
10.36: of school knowledge. Others were entirely special, usable only with the children of this particular school on this particular d
10.37: ay. Not all of the questions were put in the same terms, and a given response did not always receive the same score. When the ch
10.38: ildren responded incorrectly or incompletely, they were often given help, but not always to the same extent. In other words, say
10.39: s Binet, it was evident that "the teachers employed very awkwardly a very excellent method." The above remark is as pertinent as
10.40: it is expressive. As the statement implies, the test method is but a refinement and standardization of the commonsense approach
10.41: . Binet remarks that most people who inquire into his method of measuring intelligence do so expecting to find something very su
10.42: rprising and mysterious; and on seeing how much it resembles the methods which common sense employs in ordinary life, they heave
10.43: a sigh of disappointment and say, "Is that all?" Binet reminds us that the difference between the scientific and unscientific w
10.44: ay of doing a thing is not necessarily a difference in the _nature_ of the method; it is often merely a difference in _exactness
10.45: _. Science does the thing better, because it does it more accurately. It was of course not the purpose of Binet to cast a slur u
10.46: pon the good sense and judgment of teachers. The teachers who took part in the little experiment described above were Binet's pe
10.47: rsonal friends. The errors he points out in his entertaining and goodhumored account of the experiment are inherent in the situa
10.48: tion. They are the kind of errors which any person, however discriminating and observant, is likely to make in estimating the in
10.49: telligence of a subject without the use of standardized tests. It is the writer's experience that the teacher's estimate of a ch
10.50: ild's intelligence is much more reliable than that of the average parent; more accurate even than that of the physician who has
10.51: not had psychological training. Indeed, it is an exceptional school physician who is able to give any very valuable assistance t
10.52: o teachers in the classification of mentally exceptional children for special pedagogical treatment. This is only to be expected
10.53: , for the physician has ordinarily had much less instruction in psychology than the teacher, and of course infinitely less exper
10.54: ience in judging the mental performances of children. Even if graduated from a firstrank medical school, the instruction he has
10.55: received in the important subject of mental deficiency has probably been less adequate than that given to the students of a stan
10.56: dard normal school. As a rule, the doctor has no equipment or special fitness which gives him any advantage over the teacher in
10.57: acquiring facility in the use of intelligence tests. As for parents, it would of course be unreasonable to expect from them a ve
10.58: ry accurate judgment regarding the mental peculiarities of their children. The difficulty is not simply that which comes from la
10.59: ck of special training. The presence of parental affection renders impartial judgment impossible. Still more serious are the eff
10.60: ects of habituation to the child's mental traits. As a result of such habituation the most intelligent parent tends to develop a
10.61: n unfortunate blindness to all sorts of abnormalities which exist in his own children. The only way of escape from the fallacies
10.62: we have mentioned lies in the use of some kind of refined psychological procedure. Binet testing is destined to become universa
10.63: lly known and practiced in schools, prisons, reformatories, charity stations, orphan asylums, and even ordinary homes, for the s
10.64: ame reason that Babcock testing has become universal in dairying. Each is indispensable to its purpose. CHAPTER III DESCRIPTION

11.1: OF THE BINETSIMON METHOD ESSENTIAL NATURE OF THE SCALE. The Binet scale is made up of an extended series of tests in the nature
11.2: of "stunts," or problems, success in which demands the exercise of intelligence. As left by Binet, the scale consists of 54 test
11.3: s, so graded in difficulty that the easiest lie well within the range of normal 3yearold children, while the hardest tax the int
11.4: elligence of the average adult. The problems are designed primarily to test native intelligence, not school knowledge or home tr
11.5: aining. They try to answer the question "How intelligent is this child?" How much the child has learned is of significance only
11.6: in so far as it throws light on his ability to learn more. Binet fully appreciated the fact that intelligence is not homogeneous
11.7: , that it has many aspects, and that no one kind of test will display it adequately. He therefore assembled for his intelligence
11.8: scale tests of many different types, some of them designed to display differences of memory, others differences in power to rea
11.9: son, ability to compare, power of comprehension, time orientation, facility in the use of number concepts, power to combine idea
11.10: s into a meaningful whole, the maturity of apperception, wealth of ideas, knowledge of common objects, etc. HOW THE SCALE WAS DE
11.11: RIVED. The tests were arranged in order of difficulty, as found by trying them upon some 200 normal children of different ages f
11.12: rom 3 to 15 years. It was found, for illustration, that a certain test was passed by only a very small proportion of the younger
11.13: children, say the 5yearolds, and that the number passing this test increased rapidly in the succeeding years until by the age o
11.14: f 7 or 8 years, let us say, practically all the children were successful. If, in our supposed case, the test was passed by about
11.15: two thirds to three fourths of the normal children aged 7 years, it was considered by Binet a test of 7year intelligence. In li
11.16: ke manner, a test passed by 65 to 75 per cent of the normal 9yearolds was considered a test of 9year intelligence, and so on. By
11.17: trying out many different tests in this way it was possible to secure five tests to represent each age from 3 to 10 years (exce
11.18: pting age 4, which has only four tests), five for age 12, five for 15, and five for adults, making 54 tests in all. LIST OF TEST
11.19: S. The following is the list of tests as arranged by Binet in 1911, shortly before his untimely death: _Age 3:_ 1. Points to nos
11.20: e, eyes, and mouth. 2. Repeats two digits. 3. Enumerates objects in a picture. 4. Gives family name. 5. Repeats a sentence of si
11.21: x syllables. _Age 4:_ 1. Gives his sex. 2. Names key, knife, and penny. 3. Repeats three digits. 4. Compares two lines. _Age 5:_
11.22: 1. Compares two weights. 2. Copies a square. 3. Repeats a sentence of ten syllables. 4. Counts four pennies. 5. Unites the halv
11.23: es of a divided rectangle. _Age 6:_ 1. Distinguishes between morning and afternoon. 2. Defines familiar words in terms of use. 3
11.24: . Copies a diamond. 4. Counts thirteen pennies. 5. Distinguishes pictures of ugly and pretty faces. _Age 7:_ 1. Shows right hand
11.25: and left ear. 2. Describes a picture. 3. Executes three commissions, given simultaneously. 4. Counts the value of six sous, thr
11.26: ee of which are double. 5. Names four cardinal colors. _Age 8:_ 1. Compares two objects from memory. 2. Counts from 20 to 0. 3.
11.27: Notes omissions from pictures. 4. Gives day and date. 5. Repeats five digits. _Age 9:_ 1. Gives change from twenty sous. 2. Defi
11.28: nes familiar words in terms superior to use. 3. Recognizes all the pieces of money. 4. Names the months of the year, in order. 5
11.29: . Answers easy "comprehension questions." _Age 10:_ 1. Arranges five blocks in order of weight. 2. Copies drawings from memory.
11.30: 3. Criticizes absurd statements. 4. Answers difficult "comprehension questions." 5. Uses three given words in not more than two
11.31: sentences. _Age 12:_ 1. Resists suggestion. 2. Composes one sentence containing three given words. 3. Names sixty words in three
11.32: minutes. 4. Defines certain abstract words. 5. Discovers the sense of a disarranged sentence. _Age 15:_ 1. Repeats seven digits
11.33: . 2. Finds three rhymes for a given word. 3. Repeats a sentence of twentysix syllables. 4. Interprets pictures. 5. Interprets gi
11.34: ven facts. _Adult:_ 1. Solves the papercutting test. 2. Rearranges a triangle in imagination. 3. Gives differences between pairs
11.35: of abstract terms. 4. Gives three differences between a president and a king. 5. Gives the main thought of a selection which he
11.36: has heard read. It should be emphasized that merely to name the tests in this way gives little idea of their nature and meaning
11.37: , and tells nothing about Binet's method of conducting the 54 experiments. In order to use the tests intelligently it is necessa
11.38: ry to acquaint one's self thoroughly with the purpose of each test, its correct procedure, and the psychological interpretation
11.39: of different types of response.[10] [10] See Part II of this volume, and References 1 and 29, for discussion and interpretation
11.40: of the individual tests. In fairness to Binet, it should also be borne in mind that the scale of tests was only a rough approxim
11.41: ation to the ideal which the author had set himself to realize. Had his life been spared a few years longer, he would doubtless
11.42: have carried the method much nearer perfection. HOW THE SCALE IS USED. By means of the Binet tests we can judge the intelligence
11.43: of a given individual by comparison with standards of intellectual performance for normal children of different ages. In order
11.44: to make the comparison it is only necessary to begin the examination of the subject at a point in the scale where all the tests
11.45: are passed successfully, and to continue up the scale until no more successes are possible. Then we compare our subject's perfor
11.46: mances with the standard for normal children of the same age, and note the amount of acceleration or retardation. Let us suppose
11.47: the subject being tested is 9 years of age. If he goes as far in the tests as normal 9yearold children ordinarily go, we can sa
11.48: y that the child has a "mental age" of 9 years, which in this case is normal (our child being 9 years of age). If he goes only a
11.49: s far as normal 8yearold children ordinarily go, we say that his "mental age" is 8 years. In like manner, a mentally defective c
11.50: hild of 9 years may have a "mental age" of only 4 years, or a young genius of 9 years may have a mental age of 12 or 13 years. S
11.51: PECIAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE BINETSIMON METHOD. Psychologists had experimented with intelligence tests for at least twenty year
11.52: s before the Binet scale made its appearance. The question naturally suggests itself why Binet should have been successful in a
11.53: field where previous efforts had been for the most part futile. The answer to this question is found in three essential differen
11.54: ces between Binet's method and those formerly employed. 1. _The use of age standards._ Binet was the first to utilize the idea o
11.55: f age standards, or norms, in the measurement of intelligence. It will be understood, of course, that Binet did not set out to i
11.56: nvent tests of 10year intelligence, 6year intelligence, etc. Instead, as already explained, he began with a series of tests rang
11.57: ing from very easy to very difficult, and by trying these tests on children of different ages and noting the percentages of succ
11.58: esses in the various years, he was able to locate them (approximately) in the years where they belonged. This plan has the great
11.59: advantage of giving us standards which are easily grasped. To say, for illustration, that a given subject has a grade of intell
11.60: igence equal to that of the average child of 8 years is a statement whose general import does not need to be explained. Previous
11.61: investigators had worked with subjects the degree of whose intelligence was unknown, and with tests the difficulty of which was
11.62: equally unknown. An immense amount of ingenuity was spent in devising tests which were used in such a way as to preclude any ve
11.63: ry meaningful interpretation of the responses. The Binet method enables us to characterize the intelligence of a child in a far
11.64: more definite way than had hitherto been possible. Current descriptive terms like "bright," "moderately bright," "dull," "very d

12.1: ull," "feebleminded," etc., have had no universally accepted meaning. A child who is designated by one person as "moderately bri
12.2: ght" may be called "very bright" by another person. The degree of intelligence which one calls "moderate dullness," another may
12.3: call "extreme dullness," etc. But every one knows what is meant by the term 8year mentality, 4year mentality, etc., even if he i
12.4: s not able to define these grades of intelligence in psychological terms; and by ascertaining experimentally what intellectual t
12.5: asks children of different ages can perform, we are, of course, able to make our age standards as definite as we please. Why sho
12.6: uld a device so simple have waited so long for a discoverer? We do not know. It is of a class with many other unaccountable myst
12.7: eries in the development of scientific method. Apparently the idea of an agegrade method, as this is called, did not come to Bin
12.8: et himself until he had experimented with intelligence tests for some fifteen years. At least his first provisional scale, publi
12.9: shed in 1905, was not made up according to the agegrade plan. It consisted merely of 30 tests, arranged roughly in order of diff
12.10: iculty. Although Binet nowhere gives any account of the steps by which this crude and ungraded scale was transformed into the re
12.11: latively complete agegrade scale of 1908, we can infer that the original and ingenious idea of utilizing age norms was suggested
12.12: by the data collected with the 1905 scale. However the discovery was made, it ranks, perhaps, from the practical point of view,
12.13: as the most important in all the history of psychology. 2. _The kind of mental functions brought into play._ In the second plac
12.14: e, the Binet tests differ from most of the earlier attempts in that they are designed to test the higher and more complex mental
12.15: processes, instead of the simpler and more elementary ones. Hence they set problems for the reasoning powers and ingenuity, pro
12.16: voke judgments about abstract matters, etc., instead of attempting to measure sensory discrimination, mere retentiveness, rapidi
12.17: ty of reaction, and the like. Psychologists had generally considered the higher processes too complex to be measured directly, a
12.18: nd accordingly sought to get at them indirectly by correlating supposed intelligence with simpler processes which could readily
12.19: be measured, such as reaction time, rapidity of tapping, discrimination of tones and colors, etc. While they were disputing over
12.20: their contradictory findings in this line of exploration, Binet went directly to the point and succeeded where they had failed.
12.21: It is now generally admitted by psychologists that higher intelligence is little concerned in such elementary processes as thos
12.22: e mentioned above. Many of the animals have keen sensory discrimination. Feebleminded children, unless of very low grade, do not
12.23: differ very markedly from normal children in sensitivity of the skin, visual acuity, simple reaction time, type of imagery, etc
12.24: . But in power of comprehension, abstraction, and ability to direct thought, in the nature of the associative processes, in amou
12.25: nt of information possessed, and in spontaneity of attention, they differ enormously. 3. _Binet would test "general intelligence
12.26: ."_ Finally, Binet's success was largely due to his abandonment of the older "faculty psychology" which, far from being defunct,
12.27: had really given direction to most of the earlier work with mental tests. Where others had attempted to measure memory attentio
12.28: n, sense discrimination, etc., as separate faculties or functions, Binet undertook to ascertain the _general level_ of intellige
12.29: nce. Others had thought the task easier of accomplishment by measuring each division or aspect of intelligence separately, and s
12.30: ummating the results. Binet, too, began in this way, and it was only after years of experimentation by the usual methods that he
12.31: finally broke away from them and undertook, so to speak, to triangulate the height of his tower without first getting the dimen
12.32: sions of the individual stones which made it up. The assumption that it is easier to measure a part, or one aspect, of intellige
12.33: nce than all of it, is fallacious in that the parts are not separate parts and cannot be separated by any refinement of experime
12.34: nt. They are interwoven and intertwined. Each ramifies everywhere and appears in all other functions. The analogy of the stones
12.35: of the tower does not really apply. Memory, for example, cannot be tested separately from attention, or sensediscrimination sepa
12.36: rately from the associative processes. After many vain attempts to disentangle the various intellective functions, Binet decided
12.37: to test their combined functional capacity without any pretense of measuring the exact contribution of each to the total produc
12.38: t. It is hardly too much to say that intelligence tests have been successful just to the extent to which they have been guided b
12.39: y this aim. Memory, attention, imagination, etc., are terms of "structural psychology." Binet's psychology is dynamic. He concei
12.40: ves intelligence as the sum total of those thought processes which consist in mental adaptation. This adaptation is not explicab
12.41: le in terms of the old mental "faculties." No one of these can explain a single thought process, for such process always involve
12.42: s the participation of many functions whose separate rôles are impossible to distinguish accurately. Instead of measuring the in
12.43: tensity of various mental states (psychophysics), it is more enlightening to measure their combined effect on adaptation. Using
12.44: a biological comparison, Binet says the old "faculties" correspond to the separate tissues of an animal or plant, while his own
12.45: "scheme of thought" corresponds to the functioning organ itself. For Binet, psychology is the science of behavior. BINET'S CONCE
12.46: PTION OF GENERAL INTELLIGENCE. In devising tests of intelligence it is, of course, necessary to be guided by some assumption, or
12.47: assumptions, regarding the nature of intelligence. To adopt any other course is to depend for success upon happy chance. Howeve
12.48: r, it is impossible to arrive at a final definition of intelligence on the basis of _apriori_ considerations alone. To demand, a
12.49: s critics of the Binet method have sometimes done, that one who would measure intelligence should first present a complete defin
12.50: ition of it, is quite unreasonable. As Stern points out, electrical currents were measured long before their nature was well und
12.51: erstood. Similar illustrations could be drawn from the processes involved in chemistry physiology, and other sciences. In the ca
12.52: se of intelligence it may be truthfully said that no adequate definition can possibly be framed which is not based primarily on
12.53: the symptoms empirically brought to light by the test method. The best that can be done in advance of such data is to make tenta
12.54: tive assumptions as to the probable nature of intelligence, and then to subject these assumptions to tests which will show their
12.55: correctness or incorrectness. New hypotheses can then be framed for further trial, and thus gradually we shall be led to a conc
12.56: eption of intelligence which will be meaningful and in harmony with all the ascertainable facts. Such was the method of Binet. O
12.57: nly those unacquainted with Binet's more than fifteen years of labor preceding the publication of his intelligence scale would t
12.58: hink of accusing him of making no effort to analyze the mental processes which his tests bring into play. It is true that many o
12.59: f Binet's earlier assumptions proved untenable, and in this event he was always ready, with exceptional candor and intellectual
12.60: plasticity, to acknowledge his error and to plan a new line of attack. Binet's conception of intelligence emphasizes three chara
12.61: cteristics of the thought process: (1) Its tendency to take and maintain a definite direction; (2) the capacity to make adaptati

12.63: e des imbeciles," in _L'Année Psychologique_ (1909), pp. 1147. The last division of this article is devoted to a discussion of t

13.5: different combinations under the influence of this directing idea, which guides the efforts of the subject even though he may n
13.6: ot be conscious of the fact; and (3) to judge the combination which has been made, to compare it with the model, and to decide w
13.7: hether it is the correct one." [12] See especially pages 162 and 238. Much the same processes are called for in many other of th
13.8: e Binet tests, particularly those of arranging weights, rearranging dissected sentences, drawing a diamond or square from copy,
13.9: finding a sentence containing three given words, counting backwards, etc. However, an examination of the scale will show that th
13.10: e choice of tests was not guided entirely by any single formula as to the nature of intelligence. Binet's approach was a manysid
13.11: ed one. The scale includes tests of time orientation, of three or four kinds of memory, of apperception, of language comprehensi
13.12: on, of knowledge about common objects, of free association, of number mastery, of constructive imagination, and of ability to co
13.13: mpare concepts, to see contradictions, to combine fragments into a unitary whole, to comprehend abstract terms, and to meet nove
13.14: l situations. OTHER CONCEPTIONS OF INTELLIGENCE. It is interesting to compare Binet's conception of intelligence with the defini
13.15: tions which have been offered by other psychologists. According to Ebbinghaus, for example, the essence of intelligence lies in
13.16: comprehending together in a unitary, meaningful whole, impressions and associations which are more or less independent, heteroge
13.17: neous, or even partly contradictory. "Intellectual ability consists in the elaboration of a whole into its worth and meaning by
13.18: means of manysided combination, correction, and completion of numerous kindred associations.... It is a _combination activity_."
13.19: Meumann offers a twofold definition. From the psychological point of view, intelligence is the power of independent and creativ
13.20: e elaboration of new products out of the material given by memory and the senses. From the practical point of view, it involves
13.21: the ability to avoid errors, to surmount difficulties, and to adjust to environment. Stern defines intelligence as "the general
13.22: capacity of an individual consciously to adjust his thinking to new requirements: it is general adaptability to new problems and
13.23: conditions of life." Spearman, Hart, and others of the English school define intelligence as a "common central factor" which pa
13.24: rticipates in all sorts of special mental activities. This factor is explained in terms of a psychophysiological hypothesis of "
13.25: cortex energy," "cerebral plasticity," etc. The above definitions are only to a slight extent contradictory or inharmonious. The
13.26: y differ mainly in point of view or in the location of the emphasis. Each expresses a part of the truth, and none all of it. It
13.27: will be evident that the conception of Binet is broad enough to include the most important elements in each of the other definit
13.28: ions quoted. GUIDING PRINCIPLES IN CHOICE AND ARRANGEMENT OF TESTS. In choosing his tests Binet was guided by the conception of
13.29: intelligence which we have set forth above. Tests were devised which would presumably bring into play the various mental process
13.30: es thought to be concerned in intelligence, and then these tests were tried out on normal children of different ages. If the per
13.31: centage of passes for a given test increased but little or not at all in going from younger to older children this test was disc
13.32: arded. On the other hand, if the proportion of passes increased rapidly with age, and if children of a given age, who on other g
13.33: rounds were known to be bright, passed more frequently than children of the same age who were known to be dull, then the test wa
13.34: s judged a satisfactory test of intelligence. As we have shown elsewhere,[13] practically all of Binet's tests fulfill these req
13.35: uirements reasonably well, a fact which bears eloquent testimony to the keen psychological insight of their author. [13] See p.
13.36: 55. In arranging the tests into a system Binet's guiding principle was to find an arrangement of the tests which would cause an
13.37: average child of any given age to test "at age"; that is, the average 5yearold must show a mental age of 5 years, the average 8y
13.38: earold a mental age of 8 years, etc. In order to secure this result Binet found that his data seemed to require the location of
13.39: an individual test in that year where it was passed by about two thirds to three fourths of unselected children. It was in the a
13.40: ssembling of the tests that the most serious faults of the scale had their origin. Further investigation has shown that a great
13.41: many of the tests were misplaced as much as one year, and several of them two years. On the whole, the scale as Binet left it wa
13.42: s decidedly too easy in the lower ranges, and too difficult in the upper. As a result, the average child of 5 years was caused t
13.43: o test at not far from 6 years, the average child of 12 years not far from 11. In the Stanford revision an effort has been made
13.44: to correct this fault, along with certain other generally recognized imperfections. SOME AVOWED LIMITATIONS OF THE BINET TESTS.
13.45: The Binet tests have often been criticized for their unfitness to perform certain services which in reality they were never mean
13.46: t to render. This is unfair. We cannot make a just evaluation of the scale without bearing in mind its avowed limitations. For e
13.47: xample, the scale does not pretend to measure the entire mentality of the subject, but only _general intelligence_. There is no
13.48: pretense of testing the emotions or the will beyond the extent to which these naturally display themselves in the tests of intel
13.49: ligence. The scale was not designed as a tool for the analysis of those emotional or volitional aberrations which are concerned
13.50: in such mental disorders as hysteria, insanity, etc. These conditions do not present a progressive reduction of intelligence to
13.51: the infantile level, and in most of them other factors besides intelligence play an important rôle. Moreover, even in the normal
13.52: individual the fruitfulness of intelligence, the direction in which it shall be applied, and its methods of work are to a certa
13.53: in extent determined by the extraneous factors of emotion and volition. It should, nevertheless, be pointed out that defects of
13.54: intelligence, in a large majority of cases, also involve disturbances of the emotional and volitional functions. We do not expec
13.55: t to find perfectly normal emotions or will power of average strength coupled with marked intellectual deficiency, and as a matt
13.56: er of fact such a combination is rare indeed. In the course of an examination with the Binet tests, the experienced clinical psy
13.57: chologist is able to gain considerable insight into the subject's emotional and volitional equipment, even though the method was
13.58: designed primarily for another purpose. A second misunderstanding can be avoided by remembering that the Binet scale does not p
13.59: retend to bring to light the idiosyncrasies of special talent, but only to measure the general level of intelligence. It cannot
13.60: be used for the discovery of exceptional ability in drawing, painting, music, mathematics, oratory, salesmanship, etc., because
13.61: no effort is made to explore the processes underlying these abilities. It can, therefore, never serve as a _detailed chart_ for
13.62: the vocational guidance of children, telling us which will succeed in business, which in art, which in medicine, etc. It is not
13.63: a new kind of phrenology. At the same time, as we have already pointed out, _it is capable of bounding roughly the vocational te
13.64: rritory in which an individual's intelligence will probably permit success, nothing else preventing_.[14] [14] See p. 17. In the

14.1: third place, it must not be supposed that the scale can be used as a complete pedagogical guide. Although intelligence tests fu
14.2: rnish data of the greatest significance for pedagogical procedure, they do not suggest the appropriate educational methods in de
14.3: tail. These will have to be worked out in a practical way for the various grades of intelligence, and at great cost of labor and
14.4: patience. Finally, in arriving at an estimate of a subject's grade of intelligence and his susceptibility to training, it would
14.5: be a mistake to ignore the data obtainable from other sources. No competent psychologist, however ardent a supporter of the Bin
14.6: et method he might be, would recommend such a policy. Those who accept the method as allsufficient are as much in error as those
14.7: who consider it as no more important than any one of a dozen other approaches. Standardized tests have already become and will
14.8: remain by far the most reliable single method for grading intelligence, but the results they furnish will always need to be inte
14.9: rpreted in the light of supplementary information regarding the subject's personal history, including medical record, accidents,
14.10: play habits, industrial efficiency, social and moral traits, school success, home environment, etc. Without question, however,
14.11: the improved Binet tests will contribute more than all other data combined to the end of enabling us to forecast a child's possi
14.12: bilities of future improvement, and this is the information which will aid most in the proper direction of his education. CHAPTE

27.35: l the same tests give consistent results when used repeatedly with the same subject? In general we may say that they do. Somethi

27.38: age by the Binet scale, year after year. In their case, familiarity with the tests does not in the least improve the responses.
27.39: At each retesting the responses given at previous examinations are repeated with only the most trivial variations. Of 352 feeble
27.40: minded children tested at Vineland, three years in succession, 109 gave absolutely no variation, 232 showed a variation of not m
27.41: ore than two fifths of a year, while 22 gained as much as one year in the three tests. The latter, presumably, were younger chil
27.42: dren whose intelligence was still developing. Goddard has also tested 464 publicschool children for three successive years. Appr

27.45: of Goddard. The reapplication of the tests showed absolutely no influence of familiarity, the correlation of the two tests being

27.47: ted _plus_ in the first test advanced in the twelve months about a year and a quarter, as we should expect those to do whose men
27.48: tal development is accelerated. Correspondingly, those who tested _minus_ at the first test advanced only about three fourths of

27.51: the above findings. In this case the two tests were separated by an interval of two to four years, and the correlation between t

27.58: average improvement of little more than three months. No child varied in the second test more than half a year from the mental

27.64: e it would probably be desirable to have one or more additional scales for alternative use in testing the same children at very

28.1: brief intervals, the same scale may be used for repeated tests at intervals of a year or more with little danger of serious inac
28.2: curacy. Moreover, results like those set forth above are important evidence as to the validity of the test method. INFLUENCE OF
28.3: SOCIAL AND EDUCATIONAL ADVANTAGES. The criticism has often been made that the responses to many of the tests are so much subject
28.4: to the influence of school and home environment as seriously to invalidate the scale as a whole. Some of the tests most often n
28.5: amed in this connection are the following: Giving age and sex; naming common objects, colors, and coins; giving the value of sta
28.6: mps; giving date; naming the months of the year and the days of the week; distinguishing forenoon and afternoon; counting; makin
28.7: g change; reading for memories; naming sixty words; giving definitions; finding rhymes; and constructing a sentence containing t
28.8: hree given words. It has in fact been found wherever comparisons have been made that children of superior social status yield a
28.9: higher average mental age than children of the laboring classes. The results of Decroly and Degand and of Meumann, Stern, and Bi
28.10: net himself may be referred to in this connection. In the case of the Stanford investigation, also, it was found that when the u
28.11: nselected school children were grouped in three classes according to social status (superior, average, and inferior), the averag
28.12: e I Q for the superior social group was 107, and that of the inferior social group 93. This is equivalent to a difference of one
28.13: year in mental age with 7yearolds, and to a difference of two years with 14yearolds. However, the common opinion that the child
28.14: from a cultured home does better in tests solely by reason of his superior home advantages is an entirely gratuitous assumption
28.15: . Practically all of the investigations which have been made of the influence of nature and nurture on mental performance agree
28.16: in attributing far more to original endowment than to environments. Common observation would itself suggest that the social clas
28.17: s to which the family belongs depends less on chance than on the parents' native qualities of intellect and character. The resul
28.18: ts of five separate and distinct lines of inquiry based on the Stanford data agree in supporting the conclusion that the childre
28.19: n of successful and cultured parents test higher than children from wretched and ignorant homes for the simple reason that their
28.20: heredity is better. The results of this investigation are set forth in full elsewhere.[42] [42] See _The Stanford Revision and
28.21: Extension of the BinetSimon Measuring Scale of Intelligence_. (Warwick and York, 1916) It would, of course, be going too far to
28.22: deny all possibility of environmental conditions affecting the result of an intelligence test. Certainly no one would expect tha
28.23: t a child reared in a cage and denied all intercourse with other human beings could by any system of mental measurement test up
28.24: to the level of normal children. There is, however, no reason to believe that _ordinary_ differences in social environment (apar
28.25: t from heredity), differences such as those obtaining among unselected children attending approximately the same general type of
28.26: school in a civilized community, affects to any great extent the validity of the scale. A crucial experiment would be to take a
28.27: large number of very young children of the lower classes and, after placing them in the most favorable environment obtainable,
28.28: to compare their later mental development with that of children born into the best homes. No extensive study of this kind has be
28.29: en made, but the writer has tested twenty orphanage children who, for the most part, had come from very inferior homes. They had
28.30: been in a wellconducted orphanage for from two to several years, and had enjoyed during that time the advantages of an excellen
28.31: t village school. Nevertheless, all but three tested below average, ranging from 75 to 90 I Q. The impotence of school instructi
28.32: on to neutralize individual differences in native endowment will be evident to any one who follows the school career of backward
28.33: children. The children who are seriously retarded in school are not normal, and cannot be made normal by any refinement of educ
28.34: ational method. As a rule, the longer the inferior child attends school, the more evident his inferiority becomes. It would hard
28.35: ly be reasonable, therefore, to expect that a little incidental instruction in the home would weigh very heavily against these s
28.36: ame native differences in endowment. Cases like the following show conclusively that it does not: X is the son of unusually inte
28.37: lligent and welleducated parents. The home is everything one would expect of people of scholarly pursuits and cultivated tastes.
28.38: But X has always been irresponsible, troublesome, childish, and queer. He learned to walk at 2 years, to talk at 3, and has alw
28.39: ays been delicate and nervous. When brought for examination he was 8 years old. He had twice attempted school work, but could ac
28.40: complish nothing and was withdrawn. His playlife was not normal, and other children, younger than himself, abused and tormented
28.41: him. The Binet tests gave an I Q of approximately 75; that is, the retardation amounted to about two years. The child was examin
28.42: ed again three years later. At that time, after attending school two years, he had recently completed the first grade. This time
28.43: the I Q was 73. Strange to say, the mother is encouraged and hopeful because she sees that her boy is learning to read. She doe
28.44: s not seem to realize that at his age he ought to be within three years of entering high school. The fortyminute test had told m
28.45: ore about the mental ability of this boy than the intelligent mother had been able to learn in eleven years of daily and hourly
28.46: observation. For X is feebleminded; he will never complete the grammar school; he will never be an efficient worker or a respons
28.47: ible citizen. Let us change the picture. Z is a brighteyed, darkskinned girl of 9 years. She is darkskinned because her father i
28.48: s a mixture of Indian and Spanish. The mother is of Irish descent. With her strangely mated parents and two brothers she lives i
28.49: n a dirty, cramped, and poorly furnished house in the country. The parents are illiterate, and the brothers are retarded and dul
28.50: l, though not feebleminded. It is Z's turn to be tested. I inquire the name. It is familiar, for I have already tested the two s
28.51: tupid brothers. I also know her ignorant parents and the miserable cabin in which she lives. The examination begins with the 8ye
28.52: ar tests. The responses are quick and accurate. We proceed to the 9year group. There is no failure, and there is but one minor e
28.53: rror. Successes and failures alternate for a while until the latter prevail. Z has tested at 11 years. In spite of her wretched
28.54: home, she is mentally advanced nearly 25 per cent. By the vocabulary test she is credited with a knowledge of nearly 6000 words,
28.55: or nearly four times as many as X, the boy of cultured home and scholarly parents, had learned by the age of 8 years. Five year
28.56: s have passed. When given the test, Z was in the fourth grade and, as we have already stated, 9 years of age. As a result of the
28.57: test she was transferred to the fifth grade. Later she skipped again and at the age of 14 is a successful student in the second
28.58: year of high school. To assay her intelligence and determine its quality was a task of fortyfive minutes. The above cases, each
28.59: of which could be paralleled by many others which we have found, will serve to illustrate the fact that exceptionally superior
28.60: endowment is discoverable by the tests, however unfavorable the home from which it comes, and that inferior endowment cannot be
28.61: normalized by all the advantages of the most cultured home. Quoting again from Stern, "The tests actually reach and discover the
28.62: general developmental conditions of intelligence, and not mere fragments of knowledge and attainments acquired by chance." PART
28.63: II GUIDE FOR THE USE OF THE STANFORD REVISION AND EXTENSION CHAPTER VIII GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS NECESSITY OF SECURING ATTENTION A
28.64: ND EFFORT. The child's intelligence is to be judged by his success in the performance of certain tasks. These tasks may appear t

29.1: o the examiner to be very easy, indeed; but we must bear in mind that they are often anything but easy for the child. Real effor
29.2: t and attention are necessary for his success, and occasionally even his best efforts fall short of the desired result. If the t
29.3: ests are to display the child's real intellectual ability it will be necessary, therefore, to avoid as nearly as possible every
29.4: disturbing factor which would divide his attention or in any other way injure the quality of his responses. To insure this it wi
29.5: ll be necessary to consider somewhat in detail a number of factors which influence effort, such as degree of quiet, the nature o
29.6: f surroundings, presence or absence of others, means of gaining the child's confidence, the avoidance of embarrassment, fatigue,
29.7: etc. One should not expect, however, to secure an absolutely equal degree of attention from all subjects. The power to give sus
29.8: tained attention to a difficult task is characteristically weak in dull and feebleminded children. What we should labor to secur
29.9: e is the maximum attention of which the child is capable, and if this is unsatisfactory without external cause, we are to regard
29.10: the fact as symptomatic of inferior mental ability, not as an extenuating factor or an excuse for lack of success in the tests.
29.11: Attention, of course, cannot be normal if any acute physical or mental disturbance is present. Toothache, headache, earache, na
29.12: usea, fever, cold, etc., all render the test inadvisable. The same is true of mental anxiety or fear, as in the case of the chil
29.13: d who has just been arrested and brought before the court. QUIET AND SECLUSION. The tests should be conducted in a quiet room, l
29.14: ocated where the noises of the street and other outside distractions cannot enter. A reasonably small room is better than a very
29.15: large one, because it is more homelike. The furnishings of the room should be simple. A table and two chairs are sufficient. If
29.16: the room contains a number of unfamiliar objects, such as psychological apparatus, pictures on the walls, etc., the attention o
29.17: f the child is likely to be drawn away from the tasks which he is given to do. The halls and corridors which it is sometimes nec
29.18: essary to use in testing school children are usually noisy, cold, or otherwise objectionable. PRESENCE OF OTHERS. A still more d
29.19: isturbing influence is the presence of other persons. Generally speaking, if accurate results are to be secured it is not permis
29.20: sible to have any auditor, besides possibly an assistant to record the responses. Even the assistant, however quiet and unobtrus
29.21: ive, is sometimes a disturbing element. Though something of a convenience, the assistant is by no means necessary, after the exa
29.22: miner has thoroughly mastered the procedure of the tests and has acquired some skill in the use of abbreviations in recording th
29.23: e answers. If an assistant or any other person is present, he should be seated somewhat behind the child, not too close, and sho
29.24: uld take no notice of the child either when he enters the room or at any time during the examination. At all events, the presenc
29.25: e of parent, teacher, school principal, or governess is to be avoided. Contrary to what one might expect, these distract the chi
29.26: ld much more than a strange personality would do. Their critical attitude toward the child's performance is very likely to cause
29.27: embarrassment. If the child is alone with the examiner, he is more at ease from the mere fact that he does not feel that there
29.28: is a reputation to sustain. The praise so lavishly bestowed upon him by the friendly and sympathetic examiner lends to the same
29.29: effect. As Binet emphasizes, if the presence of others cannot be avoided, it is at least necessary to require of them absolute s
29.30: ilence. Parents, and sometimes teachers, have an almost irrepressible tendency to interrupt the examination with excuses for the
29.31: child's failures and with disturbing explanations which are likely to aid the child in comprehending the required task. Without
29.32: the least intention of doing so, they sometimes practically tell the child how to respond. Parents, especially, cannot refrain
29.33: from scolding the child or showing impatience when his answers do not come up to expectation. This, of course, endangers the chi
29.34: ld's success still further. The psychologist is not surprised at such conduct. It would be foolish to expect average parents, ev
29.35: en apart from their bias in the particular case at hand, to adopt the scientific attitude of the trained examiner. Since we cann
29.36: ot in a few moments at our disposal make them over into psychologists, our only recourse is to deal with them by exclusion. This
29.37: is not to say that it is impossible to test a child satisfactorily in the presence of others. If the examiner is experienced, a
29.38: nd if the child is not timid, it is sometimes possible to make a successful test in the presence of quite a number of auditors,
29.39: provided they remain silent, refrain from staring, and otherwise conduct themselves with discretion. But not even the veteran ex
29.40: aminer can always be sure of the outcome in demonstration testing. GETTING INTO "RAPPORT." The examiner's first task is to win t
29.41: he confidence of the child and overcome his timidity. Unless _rapport_ has first been established, the results of the first test
29.42: s given are likely to be misleading. The time and effort necessary for accomplishing this are variable factors, depending upon t
29.43: he personality of both the examiner and the subject. In a majority of cases from three to five minutes should be sufficient, but
29.44: in a few cases somewhat more time is necessary. The writer has found that when a strange child is brought to the clinic for exa
29.45: mination, it is advantageous to go out of doors with him for a little walk around the university buildings. It is usually possib
29.46: le to return from such a stroll in a few minutes, with the child chattering away as though to an old friend. Another approach is
29.47: to begin by showing the child some interesting object, such as a toy, or a formboard, or pictures not used in the test. The onl
29.48: y danger in this method is that the child is likely to find the object so interesting that he may not be willing to abandon it f
29.49: or the tests, or that his mind will keep reverting to it during the examination. Still another method is to give the child his s
29.50: eat as soon as he is ushered into the room, and, after a word of greeting, which must be spoken in a kindly tone but without gus
29.51: hiness, to open up a conversation about matters likely to be of interest. The weather, place of residence, pets, sports, games,
29.52: toys, travels, current events, etc., are suitable topics if rightly employed. When the child has begun to express himself withou
29.53: t timidity and it is clear that his confidence has been gained, one may proceed, as though in continuance of the conversation, t
29.54: o inquire the name, age, and school grade. The examiner notes these down in the appropriate blanks, rather unconcernedly, at the
29.55: same time complimenting the child (unless it is clearly a case of serious retardation) on the fine progress he has made with hi
29.56: s studies. KEEPING THE CHILD ENCOURAGED. Nothing contributes more to a satisfactory _rapport_ than praise of the child's efforts
29.57: . Under no circumstances should the examiner permit himself to show displeasure at a response, however absurd it may be. In gene
29.58: ral, the poorer the response, the better satisfied one should appear to be with it. An error is always to be passed by without c
29.59: omment, unless it is painfully evident to the child himself, in which case the examiner will do well to make some excuse for it;
29.60: e.g., "You are not quite old enough to answer questions like that one; but, never mind, you are doing beautifully," etc. Exclam
29.61: ations like "fine!" "splendid!" etc., should be used lavishly. Almost any innocent deception is permissible which keeps the chil
29.62: d interested, confident, and at his best level of effort. The examination should begin with tests that are fairly easy, in order
29.63: to give the child a little experience with success before the more difficult tests are reached. THE IMPORTANCE OF TACT. It goes
29.64: without saying that children's personalities are not so uniform and simple that we can adhere always to a single stereotyped pr

30.1: ocedure in working our way into their good graces. Suggestions like the above have their value, but, like rules of etiquette, th
30.2: ey must be supported by the tact which comes of intuition and cannot be taught. The address which flatters and pleases one child
30.3: may excite disgust in another. The examiner must scent the situation and adapt his method to it. One child is timid and embarra
30.4: ssed; another may think his mental powers are under suspicion and so react with sullen obstinacy; a third may be in an angry moo
30.5: d as a result of a recent playground quarrel. Situations like these are, of course, exceptional, but in any case it is necessary
30.6: to create in the child a certain mood, or indefinable attitude of mind, before the test begins. PERSONALITY OF THE EXAMINER. Do
30.7: ubtless there are persons so lacking in personal adaptability that success in this kind of work would be for them impossible. Th
30.8: e wooden, mechanical, matteroffact and unresponsive personality is as much out of place in the psychological clinic as the tradi
30.9: tional bull in the china shop. It would make an interesting study for some one to investigate, by exact methods, the influence o
30.10: n test results of the personality of different examiners who have been equally trained in the methods to be employed and who are
30.11: equally conscientious in applying them according to rules. On the whole, differences of this kind are probably not very great a
30.12: mong experienced and reasonably competent examiners. Adaptability grows with experience and with increase of selfconfidence. Aft
30.13: er a few score tests there should be no serious failure from inability to get into _rapport_ with the child. Even in those rare
30.14: cases where the child breaks down and cries from timidity, or perhaps refuses to answer out of embarrassment, the difficulty can
30.15: be overcome by sufficient tact so that the examination may proceed as though nothing had happened. If the examiner has the prop
30.16: er psychological and personal equipment, the testing of twenty or thirty children forms a fairly satisfactory apprenticeship. Wi
30.17: thout psychological training, no amount of experience will guarantee absolute accuracy of the results. THE AVOIDANCE OF FATIGUE.
30.18: Against the validity of intelligence tests it is often argued that the result of an examination depends a great deal on the tim
30.19: e of day when it is made, whether in the morning hours when the mind is at its best, or in the afternoon when it is supposedly f
30.20: atigued. Although no very extensive investigation has been made of this influence, there is no evidence that the ordinary fatigu
30.21: e incident to school work injures the child's performance appreciably. Our tests of 1000 children showed no inferiority of resul
30.22: ts secured from 1 to 4 P.M., as compared with tests made from 9 to 12 A.M. An explanation for this is not hard to find. Although
30.23: school work causes fatigue, in the sense that a part of the child's available supply of mental energy is used up, there is alwa
30.24: ys a reserve of energy sufficient to carry the child through a thirtyto fiftyminute test. The fact that the required tasks are n
30.25: ovel and interesting to a high degree insures that the reserve energy will really be brought into play. This principle, of cours
30.26: e, has its natural limits. The examiner would avoid testing a child who was exhausted either from work or play, or a child who w
30.27: as noticeably sleepy. DURATION OF THE EXAMINATION. About the only danger of fatigue lies in making the examination too long. You
30.28: ng children show symptoms of weariness much more quickly than older children, and it is therefore fortunate that not so much tim
30.29: e is needed for testing them. The following allowances of time will usually be found sufficient: Children  35 years old
30.31: ts                          6090    " This allowance ordinarily includes the time necessary for getting into _rapport_ with the
30.32: child, in addition to that actually consumed in the tests. But the examiner need not expect to hold fast to any schedule. Some s

30.34: wly, but exceptions to this rule are not uncommon. One 8yearold boy examined by the writer answered so hesitatingly that it requ
30.35: ired two sittings of nearly an hour each to complete the test. The result, however, showed a mental age of 11½ years, or an I Q
30.36: of 143. It is permissible to hurry the child by an occasional "that's fine; now, quickly," etc., but in doing this caution must

30.41: e purse, and the pictures, colors, stamps, and designs for drawing should be mounted on stiff cardboard which may be punched and

30.45: rd booklet which has been specially devised for testing with the Stanford revision. It contains all the necessary printed materi
