30.47: ying, etc., and in addition gives with each test the standard for scoring. It is so arranged as to afford ample room for a _verb
30.48: atim_ record of all the child's responses, and contains other features calculated to make testing easy and accurate. Regarding p
30.49: urchasing of supplies see p. 141. Besides saving valuable time, a little methodical foresight of this kind adds to the success o
30.50: f the test. If the child is kept waiting, the test loses its interest and attention strays. See to it, if possible, that no lull
30.51: occurs in the performance. Inexperienced examiners sometimes waste time foolishly by stopping to instruct the child on his fail
30.52: ures. This is doubly bad, for besides losing time it makes the child conscious of the imperfection of his responses and creates
30.53: embarrassment. Adhere to the purpose of the test, which is to ascertain the child's intellectual level, not to instruct him. DES
30.54: IRABLE RANGE OF TESTING. There are two considerations here of equal importance. It is necessary to make the examination thorough
30.55: , but in the pursuit of thoroughness we must be careful not to produce fatigue or ennui. Unless there is reason to suspect menta
30.56: l retardation, it is usually best to begin with the group of tests just below the child's age. However, if there is a failure in
30.57: the tests of that group, it is necessary to go back and try all the tests of the previous group. In like manner the examination
30.58: should be carried up the scale, until a test group has been found in which all the tests are failed. It must be admitted, howev
30.59: er, that because of time limitations and fatigue, it is not always practicable to adhere to this ideal of thoroughness. In testi
30.60: ng normal children, little error will result if we go back no farther than the year which yielded only one failure, and if we st
30.61: op with the year in which there was only one success. _This is the lowest permissible limit of thoroughness._ Defectives are mor
30.62: e uneven mentally than normal children, and therefore scatter their successes and failures over a wider range. With such subject
30.63: s it is absolutely imperative that the test be thorough. In the case of defectives it is sometimes necessary to begin with rando
30.64: m testing, until a rough idea is gained of the mental level. But the skilled observer soon becomes able to utilize symptoms in t

31.1: he child's conversation and conduct and to dispense with most of this preliminary exploration. ORDER OF GIVING THE TESTS. The ch
31.2: ild's efforts in the tests are sometimes markedly influenced by the order in which they are given. If language tests or memory t
31.3: ests are given first, the child is likely to be embarrassed. More suitable to begin with are those which test knowledge or judgm
31.4: ent about objective things, such as the pictures, weights, stamps, bowknot, colors, coins, counting pennies, number of fingers,
31.5: right and left, time orientation, ball and field, paperfolding, etc. Tests like naming sixty words, finding rhymes, giving diffe
31.6: rences or similarities, making sentences, repeating sentences, and drawing are especially unsuitable because they tend to provok
31.7: e selfconsciousness. The tests as arranged in this revision are in the order which it is usually best to follow, but one should
31.8: not hesitate to depart from the order given when it seems best in a given case to do so. It is necessary to be constantly alert
31.9: so that when the child shows a tendency to balk at a given type of test, such as those of memory, language, numbers, drawing, "c
31.10: omprehension," etc., the work can be shifted to more agreeable tasks. When the child is at his ease again, it is usually possibl
31.11: e to return to the troublesome tests with better success. In the case of 8yearold D. C., who is a speech defective but otherwise
31.12: above normal, it was quite impossible at the first sitting to give such tests as sentencemaking, naming sixty words, reading, r
31.13: epeating sentences, giving definitions, etc.; at each test of this type the child's voice broke and he was ready to cry, due, no
31.14: doubt, to sensitiveness regarding his speech defect. Others do everything willingly except the drawing and copying. The younger
31.15: children sometimes refuse to repeat the sentences or digits. In all such cases it is best to pass on to something else. After a
31.16: few minutes the rejected task may be done willingly. COAXING TO BE AVOIDED. Although we should always encourage the child to be
31.17: lieve that he can answer correctly, if he will only try, we must avoid the common practice of dragging out responses by too much
31.18: urging and coaxing. The sympathies of the examiner tend to lead him into the habit of repeating and explaining the question if
31.19: the child does not answer promptly. This is nearly always a mistake, for the question is one which should be understood. Besides
31.20: , explanations and coaxing are too often equivalent to answering the question for the child. It is almost impossible to impress
31.21: this danger sufficiently upon the untrained examiner. One who is not familiar with the psychology of suggestion may put the answ
31.22: er in the child's mouth without suspecting what he is doing. ADHERING TO FORMULA. It cannot be too strongly emphasized that unle
31.23: ss we follow a standardized procedure the tests lose their significance. The danger is chiefly that of unintentionally and uncon
31.24: sciously introducing variations which will affect the meaning of the test. One who has not had a thorough training in the method
31.25: s of mental testing cannot appreciate how numerous are the opportunities for the unconscious transformation of a test. Many of t
31.26: hese are pointed out in the description of the individual tests, but it would be folly to undertake to warn the experimenter aga
31.27: inst every possible error of this kind. Sometimes the omission or the addition of a single phrase in giving the test will alter
31.28: materially the significance of the response. Only the trained psychologist can vary the formula without risk of invalidating the
31.29: result, and even he must be on his guard. All sorts of misunderstandings regarding the correct placing of tests and regarding t
31.30: heir accuracy or inaccuracy have come about through the failure of different investigators to follow the same procedure. One who
31.31: would use the tests for any serious purpose, therefore, must study the procedure for each and every test until he knows it thor
31.32: oughly. After that a considerable amount of practice is necessary before one learns to avoid slips. During the early stages of p
31.33: ractice it is necessary to refer to the printed instructions frequently in order to check up errors before they have become habi
31.34: tual. The instructions hitherto available are at fault in not defining the procedure with sufficient definiteness, and it is the
31.35: purpose of this volume to make good this deficiency as far as possible. It is too much, however, to suppose that the instructio
31.36: ns can be made "foolproof." With whatever definiteness they may be set forth, situations are sure to arise which the examiner ca
31.37: nnot be formally prepared for. There is no limit to the multitude of misunderstandings possible. After testing hundreds of child
31.38: ren one still finds new examples of misapprehension. In a few such cases the instruction may be repeated, if there is reason to
31.39: think the child's hearing was at fault or if some extraordinary distraction has occurred. But unless otherwise stated in the dir
31.40: ections, the repetition of a question is ordinarily to be avoided. Supplementary explanations are hardly ever permissible. In sh
31.41: ort, numberless situations may arise in the use of a test which may injure the validity of the response, events which cannot alw
31.42: ays be dealt with by preconceived rule. Accordingly, although we must urge unceasingly the importance of following the standard
31.43: procedure, it is not to be supposed that formulas are an adequate substitute either for scientific judgment or for common sense.
31.44: SCORING. The exact method of scoring the individual tests is set forth in the following chapters. Reference to the record bookl
31.45: et for use in testing will show that the records are to be kept in detail. Each subdivision of a test should be scored separatel
31.46: y, in order that the clinical picture may be as complete as possible. This helps in the final evaluation of the results. It make
31.47: s much difference, for example, whether success in repeating six digits is earned by repeating all three correctly or only one;
31.48: or whether the child's lack of success with the absurdities is due to failure on two, three, four, or all of them. Time should b
31.49: e recorded whenever called for in the record blanks. RECORDING RESPONSES. Plus and minus signs alone are not usually sufficient.
31.50: Whenever possible the entire response should be recorded. If the test results are to be used by any other person than the exami
31.51: ner, this is absolutely essential. Any other standard of completeness opens the door to carelessness and inaccuracy. In nearly a
31.52: ll the tests, except that of naming sixty words, the examiner will find it possible by the liberal use of abbreviations to recor
31.53: d practically the entire response _verbatim_. In doing so, however, one must be careful to avoid keeping the child waiting. Occa
31.54: sionally it is necessary to leave off recording altogether because of the embarrassment sometimes aroused in the child by seeing
31.55: his answer written down. The writer has met the latter difficulty several times. When for any reason it is not feasible to reco
31.56: rd anything more than score marks, success may be indicated by the sign +, failure by , and half credit by ½. An exceptionally g
31.57: ood response may be indicated by ++ and an exceptionally poor response by . If there is a slight doubt about a success or failur
31.58: e the sign? may be added to the + or . In general, however, score the response either + or , avoiding half credit as far as it i
31.59: s possible to do so. If the entire response is not recorded it is necessary to record at least the score mark for each test _whe
31.60: n the test is given_. It must be borne in mind that the scoring is not a purely mechanical affair. Instead, the judgment of the
31.61: examiner must come into play with every record made. If the scoring is delayed, there is not only the danger of forgetting a res
31.62: ponse, but the judgment is likely to be influenced by the subject's responses to succeeding questions. Our special record bookle
31.63: t contains wide margins, so that extended notes and observations regarding the child's responses and behavior can be recorded as
31.64: the test proceeds. SCATTERING OF SUCCESSES. It is sometimes a source of concern to the untrained examiner that the successes an

32.1: d failures should be scattered over quite an extensive range of years. Why, it may be asked, should not a child who has 10year i
32.2: ntelligence answer correctly all the tests up to and including group X, and fail on all the tests beyond? There are two reasons
32.3: why such is almost never the case. In the first place, the intelligence of an individual is ordinarily not even. There are many
32.4: different kinds of intelligence, and in some of these the subject is better endowed than in others. A second reason lies in the
32.5: fact that no test can be purely and simply a test of native intelligence. Given a certain degree of intelligence, accidents of e
32.6: xperience and training bring it about that this intelligence will work more successfully with some kinds of material than with o
32.7: thers. For both of these reasons there results a scattering of successes and failures over three or four years. The subject fail
32.8: s first in one or two tests of a group, then in two or three tests of the following group, the number of failures increasing unt
32.9: il there are no successes at all. Success "tapers off" from 100 per cent to 0. Once in a great while a child fails on several of
32.10: the tests of a given year and succeeds with a majority of those in the next higher year. This is only an extreme instance of un
32.11: even intelligence or of specialized experience, and does not necessarily reflect upon the reliability of the tests for children
32.12: in general. The method of calculation given above strikes a kind of average and gives the general level of intelligence, which i
32.13: s essentially the thing we want to know. SUPPLEMENTARY CONSIDERATIONS. It would be a mistake to suppose that any set of mental t
32.14: ests could be devised which would give us complete information about a child's native intelligence. There are no tests which are
32.15: absolutely pure tests of intelligence. All are influenced to a greater or less degree also by training and by social environmen
32.16: t. For this reason, all the ascertainable facts bearing on such influences should be added to the record of the mental examinati
32.17: on, and should be given due weight in reaching a final conclusion as to the level of intelligence. The following supplementary i
32.18: nformation should be gathered, when possible: 1.  Social status (very superior, superior, average, inferior, or very inferior).
32.19: 2.  The teacher's estimate of the child's intelligence (very superior, superior, average, inferior, or very inferior). 3.  Schoo
32.20: l opportunities, including years of attendance, regularity, retardation or acceleration, etc. 4.  Quality of school work (very s
32.21: uperior, superior, average, inferior, or very inferior). 5.  Physical handicaps, if any (adenoids, diseased tonsils, partial dea
32.22: fness, imperfect vision, malnutrition, etc.). In addition, the examiner will need to take account of the general attitude of the
32.23: child during the examination. This is provided for in the record blanks under the heading "comments." The comments should descr
32.24: ibe as fully as possible the conduct and attitude of the child during the examination, with emphasis upon such disturbing factor
32.25: s as fear, timidity, unwillingness to answer, overconfidence, carelessness, lack of attention, etc. Sometimes, also, it is desir
32.26: able to verify the child's age and to make record of the verification. Once more let it be urged that no degree of mechanical pe
32.27: rfection of the tests can ever take the place of good judgment and psychological insight. Intelligence is too complicated to be
32.28: weighed, like a bag of grain, by any one who can read figures. ALTERNATIVE TESTS. The tests designated as "alternative tests" ar
32.29: e not intended for regular use. Inasmuch as they have been standardized and belong in the year group where they are placed, they
32.30: may be used as substitute tests on certain occasions. Sometimes one of the regular tests is spoiled in giving it, or the requis
32.31: ite material for it may not be at hand. Sometimes there may be reason to suspect that the subject has become acquainted with som
32.32: e of the tests. In such cases it is a great convenience to have a few substitutes available. It is necessary, however, to warn a
32.33: gainst a possible misuse of alternative tests. _It is not permissible to count success in an alternative test as offsetting fail
32.34: ure in a regular test._ This would give the subject too much leeway of failure. There are very exceptional cases, however, when
32.35: it is legitimate to break this rule; namely, when one of the regular tests would be obviously unfair to the subject being tested
32.36: . In year X, for example, one of the three alternative tests should be substituted for the reading test (X, 4) in case we are te
32.37: sting a subject who has not had the equivalent of at least two years of school work. In year VIII, it would be permissible to su
32.38: bstitute the alternative test of naming six coins, instead of the vocabulary test, in the case of a subject who came from a home
32.39: where English was not spoken. In VII, it would perhaps not be unfair to substitute the alternative test, in place of the test o
32.40: f copying a diamond, in the case of a subject who, because of timidity or embarrassment, refused to attempt the diamond. But it
32.41: would be going entirely too far to substitute an alternative test in the place of every regular test which the subject responded
32.42: to by silence. In the large majority of cases persistent silence deserves to be scored failure. Certain tests have been made al
32.43: ternatives because of their inferior value, some because the presence of other tests of similar nature in the same year rendered

33.22: about a child's intelligence status. The significance of a given number of years of retardation or acceleration depends upon the
33.23: age of the child. A 3yearold child who is retarded one year is ordinarily feebleminded; a 10yearold retarded one year is only a
33.24: little below normal. The child who at 3 years of age is retarded one year will probably be retarded two years at the age of 6,
33.25: three years at the age of 9, and four years at the age of 12. What we want to know, therefore, is the ratio existing between men
33.26: tal age and real age. This is the intelligence quotient, or I Q. To find it we simply divide mental age (expressed in years and
33.27: months) by real age (also expressed in years and months). The process is easier if we express each age in terms of months alone
33.28: before dividing. The division can, of course, be performed almost instantaneously and with much less danger of error by the use
33.29: of a slide rule or a division table. One who has to calculate many intelligence quotients should by all means use some kind of m
33.30: echanical help. HOW TO FIND THE I Q OF ADULT SUBJECTS. Native intelligence, in so far as it can be measured by tests now availab
33.31: le, appears to improve but little after the age of 15 or 16 years. It follows that in calculating the I Q of an adult subject, i
33.32: t will be necessary to disregard the years he has lived beyond the point where intelligence attains its final development. Altho
33.33: ugh the location of this point is not exactly known, it will be sufficiently accurate for our purpose to assume its location at
33.34: 16 years. Accordingly, any person over 16 years of age, however old, is for purposes of calculating I Q considered to be just 16
33.35: years old. If a youth of 18 and a man of 60 years both have a mental age of 12 years, the I Q in each case is 12 ÷ 16, or .75.
33.36: The significance of various values of the I Q is set forth elsewhere.[44] Here it need only be repeated that 100 I Q means exact
33.37: ly average intelligence; that nearly all who are below 70 or 75 I Q are feebleminded; and that the child of 125 I Q is about as
33.38: much above the average as the highgrade feebleminded individual is below the average. For ordinary purposes all who fall between
33.39: 95 and 105 I Q may be considered as average in intelligence. [44] See Chapter VI. MATERIAL FOR USE IN TESTING. It is strongly r

33.52: ooklets. The record booklets are supplied only in packages of 25. CHAPTER IX Instructions For Year III III, 1. POINTING TO PARTS
33.53: OF THE BODY PROCEDURE. After getting the child's attention, say: "_Show me your nose._" "_Put your finger on your nose._" Same
33.54: with eyes, mouth, and hair. Tact is often necessary to overcome timidity. If two or three repetitions of the instruction fail to
33.55: bring a response, point to the child's chin or ear and say: "_Is this your nose?_" "_No?_" "_Then where is your nose?_" Sometim
33.56: es, after one has tried two or three parts of the test without eliciting any response, the child may suddenly release his inhibi
33.57: tions and answer all the questions promptly. In case of persistent refusal to respond it is best not to harass the child for an
33.58: answer, but to leave the test for a while and return to it later. This is a rule which applies generally throughout the scale. I
33.59: n the case of one exceptionally timid little girl, it was impossible to get any response by the usual procedure, but immediately
33.60: when a doll was shown the child pointed willingly to its nose, eyes, mouth, and hair. The device was successful because it with
33.61: drew the child's attention from herself and centered it upon something objective. SCORING. _Three responses out of four_ must be
33.62: correct. Instead of pointing, the child sometimes responds by winking the eyes, opening the mouth, etc., which is counted as sa
33.63: tisfactory. REMARKS. Binet's purpose in this test is to ascertain whether the subject is capable of comprehending simple languag
33.64: e. The ability to comprehend and use language is indeed one of the most reliable indications of the grade of mental development.

34.1: The appreciation of gestures comes first, then the comprehension of language heard, next the ability to repeat words and senten

34.7: MING FAMILIAR OBJECTS PROCEDURE. Use a key, a penny, a closed knife, a watch, and an ordinary lead pencil. The key should be the
34.8: usual largesized doorkey, not one of the Yale type. The penny should not be too new, for the freshly made, untarnished penny re
34.9: sembles very little the penny usually seen. Any ordinary pocket knife may be used, and it is to be shown unopened. The formula i
34.10: s, "_What is this?_" or, "_Tell me what this is._" SCORING. There must be at least _three correct responses out of five_. A resp
34.11: onse is not correct unless the object is named. It is not sufficient for the child merely to show that he knows its use. A child
34.12: , for example, may take the pencil and begin to mark with it, or go to the door and insert the key in the lock, but this is not
34.13: sufficient. At the same time we must not be too arbitrary about requiring a particular name. "Cent" or "pennies" for "penny" is
34.14: satisfactory, but "money" is not. The watch is sometimes called "a clock" or "a ticktock," and we shall perhaps not be too liber
34.15: al if we score these responses _plus_. "Pen" for "pencil," however, is unsatisfactory. Substitute names for "key" and "knife" ar
34.16: e rarely given. Mispronunciations due to babytalk are of course ignored. REMARKS. The purpose of this test is to find out whethe
34.17: r the child has made the association between familiar objects and their names. The mental processes necessary to enable the chil

34.19: tly seen is a form of mental activity in which the normally endowed child of 2 to 4 years finds great satisfaction. Any marked r
34.20: etardation in making such associations is a grave indication of the lack of that spontaneity which is so necessary for the devel
34.21: opment of the higher grades of intelligence. It would be entirely beside the point, therefore, to question the validity of the t
34.22: est on the ground that a given child may not have been _taught_ the names of the objects used. Practically all children 3 years

34.25: been standardized. Any improvised selection would be sure to contain some objects either less or more familiar than those in th
34.26: e standardized list. Note also that three correct responses out of five are sufficient. If we required five correct answers out
34.27: of six (like Kuhlmann), or three out of three (like Binet, Goddard, and Huey), the test would probably belong at the 4year level

39.47: e instructions with a little urging. Say nothing about hurrying, as this is likely to cause confusion. Give three trials, of one

39.49: cesses in three trials. If the first trial is a failure, move the cut halves back to their original position and say: "_No; put
39.50: them together so they will look like this_" (pointing to the uncut card). Make no other comment of approval or disapproval. Disr

39.52: turned over, the task becomes impossible, and it is then necessary to turn the piece back to its original position and begin ov

39.62: combination, compare it with the model, and decide whether it is the correct one." It may be classed, therefore, as one of the

40.49: nd down, above and below, before and behind, etc., and arrives at a knowledge of right and left rather tardily. How may we expla
40.50: in the late distinction of right and left as compared with up and down? At least four theories may be advanced: (1) Something de
40.51: pends on the frequency with which children have occasion to make the respective distinctions. (2) It may be explained on the sup
40.52: position that kinæsthetic sensations are more prominently involved in distinctions of up and down than in distinctions of right

40.57: the two aspects easily blend, while the two aspects corresponding to above and below are not viewed in such rapid succession an
40.58: d so remain much more distinct from one another in the child's mind. Or, (4), the difference may be mainly a matter of language.

44.32: EATING FIVE DIGITS PROCEDURE. Use: 31759; 42385; 98176. Tell the child to listen and to say after you just what you say. Then re
44.33: ad the first series of digits at a slightly faster rate than one per second, in a distinct voice, and with perfectly uniform emp
44.34: hasis. _Avoid rhythm._ In previous tests with digits, it was permissible to reread the first series if the child refused to resp
44.35: ond. In this year, and in the digits tests of later years, this is not permissible. Warning is not given as to the number of dig
44.36: its to be repeated. Before reading each series, get the child's attention. Do not stare at the child during the response, as thi
44.37: s is disconcerting. Look aside or at the record sheet. SCORING. Passed if the child repeats correctly, after a single reading, _
44.38: one series out of the three_ series given. The order must be correct. REMARKS. Psychologically the repetition of digits differs
44.39: from the repetition of sentences mainly in the fact that digits have less meaning (fewer associations) than the words of a sente
44.40: nce. It is because they are not as well knit together in meaning that three digits tax the memory as much as six syllables makin
44.41: g up a sentence. Testing auditory memory for digits is one of the oldest of intelligence tests. It is easy to give and lends its
44.42: elf well to exact quantitative standardization. Its value has been questioned, however, on two grounds: (1) That it is not a tes
44.43: t of pure memory, but depends largely on attention; and (2) that the results are too much influenced by the child's type of imag
44.44: ery. As to the first objection, it is true that more than one mental function is brought into play by the test. The same may be
44.45: said of every other test in the Binet scale and for that matter of any test that could be devised. It is impossible to isolate a
44.46: ny function for separate testing. In fact, the functions called memory, attention, perception, judgment, etc., never operate in
44.47: isolation. There are no separate and special "faculties" corresponding to such terms, which are merely convenient names for char
44.48: acterizing mental processes of various types. In any test it is "general ability" which is operative, perhaps now _chiefly_ in r
44.49: emembering, at another time _chiefly_ in sensory discrimination, again in reasoning, etc. The second objection, that the test is
44.50: largely invalidated by the existence of imagery types, is not borne out by the facts. Experiments have shown that pure imagery
44.51: types are exceedingly rare, and that children, especially, are characterized by "mixed" imagery. There are probably few subjects
44.52: so lacking in auditory imagery as to be placed at a serious disadvantage in this test. Lengthening a series by the addition of
44.53: a single digit adds greatly to the difficulty. While four digits can usually be repeated by children of 4 years, five digits bel
44.54: ong in year VII and six in year X. It is always interesting to note the type of errors made. The most common error is to omit on
44.55: e or more of the digits, usually in the first part of the series. If the child's ability is decidedly below the test he may give
44.56: only the last two or three out of the five or six heard. Substitutions are also quite frequent, and if so many substitutions ar
44.57: e made as to give a series quite unlike that which the child has heard, it is an unfavorable sign, indicating weakness of the cr
44.58: itical sense which is so often found with lowlevel intelligence. In case of extreme weakness of the power of autocriticism, the
44.59: child in response to the series 98176, may say 123456, or perhaps merely a couple of digits like 86, and still express complete
44.60: satisfaction with his absurd response. After each series, therefore, the examiner should say, "_Was it right?_"[54] Very young s
44.61: ubjects, however, have a tendency to answer "yes" to any question of this type, and it is therefore best not to call for critici
44.62: sm of a performance below the age of 6 or 7 years. [54] "_Was it wrong?_" is not an equivalent question and should not be used.
44.63: Digit series of a given length are not always of equal difficulty, and for this reason it is never wise to use series improvised
44.64: at the moment of the experiment. We must avoid especially series of regularly ascending or descending value, the repetition at

45.1: regular intervals of a particular digit, and all other peculiarities of arrangement which would favor the grouping of the digits
45.2: for easier retention. It remains to mention two or three further cautions in regard to procedure. It is best to begin with a se
45.3: ries about one digit below the child's expected ability. If the child has a probable intelligence of about 6 or 7 years, we shou
45.4: ld begin with four digits; in case of probable 10year intelligence we begin with five digits, etc. On the other hand, we should
45.5: avoid beginning too far down, because then the result is too much complicated by the effects of practice and fatigue. It is not
45.6: necessary, and often it is not expedient, to give the digits tests of all the different years in succession; that is, without ot
45.7: her tests intervening. While this may be permissible with older children, in young children the power of sustained attention is
45.8: so weak that no single kind of test should occupy more than two or three minutes. Children below 6 or 7 years should ordinarily
45.9: be given the tests in the order in which they are listed in the record booklet. In his 1911 revision of the scale Binet unfortun
45.10: ately shifted this test from year VII to year VIII. Goddard follows his example, but Kuhlmann retains it in year VII. The data f
45.11: rom more than a dozen leading investigations in America, England, and Germany agree in showing that the test should remain in ye

45.13: "double bow," with wings not over three or four inches long. Make this ready in advance of the experiment and show the child on
45.14: ly the completed knot. Place the model before the subject with the wings pointing to the right and left, and say: "_You know wha
45.15: t kind of knot this is, don't you? It is a bowknot. I want you to take this other piece of string and tie the same kind of knot
45.16: around my finger._" At the same time give the child a piece of shoestring, of the same length as that which is tied around the s
45.17: tick, and hold out a finger pointed toward the child and in convenient position for the operation. It is better to have the subj
45.18: ect tie the string around the examiner's finger than around a pencil or other object because the latter often falls out of the s
45.19: tring and is otherwise awkward to handle. Some children who assert that they do not know how to tie a bowknot are sometimes neve

45.21: if a double bowknot (both ends folded in) is made _in not more than a minute_. A single bowknot (only one end folded in) counts
45.22: half credit, because children are often accustomed to use the single bow altogether. The usual plain common knot, which precede
45.23: s the bowknot proper, must not be omitted if the response is to count as satisfactory, for without this preliminary plain knot a
45.24: bowknot will not hold and is of no value. To be satisfactory the knot should also be drawn up reasonably close, not left gaping

45.30: sed it. Only 35 per cent of the 6yearolds succeeded, but after that age the per cent passing increased rapidly to 94 per cent at

64.16: tract meanings and the intellectual processes by which we arrive at them. Unlike such words as _tree_, _house_, etc., the ideas

65.3: MARKS. This is an excellent test. It involves no knowledge which may not be presupposed at the age in which it is given, and suc
65.4: cess therefore depends very little on experience. The worst that can be urged against it is that it may possibly be influenced t
65.5: o a certain extent by the amount of reading the subject has done. But this has not been demonstrated. At any rate, the test sati
65.6: sfies the most important requirement of a test of intelligence; namely, the percentage of successes increases rapidly and steadi

65.8: et tells us, in fact, that it was directly suggested by the experiment of Ebbinghaus. As will readily be observed, however, it d

69.64: a piece from the folded side and ask how many holes there will be when the paper is unfolded. After recording the answer, unfol

78.1: n the problem finds himself involved in a difficulty from which he must extricate himself. Means must be found to overcome an ob
78.2: stacle. This requires practical judgement and a certain amount of inventive ingenuity. Various possibilities must be explored an
78.3: d either accepted for trial or rejected. If the amount of invention called for seems to the reader inconsiderable, let it be rem
78.4: embered that the important inventions of history have not as a rule had a Minerva birth, but instead have developed by successiv
78.5: e stages, each involving but a small step in advance. It is unnecessary to emphasize at length the function of invention in the
78.6: higher thought processes. In one form or another it is present in all intellectual activity; in the creation and use of language
78.7: , in art, in social adjustments, in religion, and in philosophy, as truly as in the domains of science and practical affairs. Ce
78.8: rtainly this is true if we accept Mason's broad definition of invention as including "every change in human activity made design
78.9: edly and systematically."[78] From the psychological point of view, perhaps, Mason is justified in looking upon the great invent
78.10: or as "an epitome of the genius of the world." To develop a KragJoergensen from a bow and arrow, a "velvettipped" lucifer match
78.11: from the primitive firestick, or a modern piano from the first crude, stringed, musical instrument has involved much the same in
78.12: tellectual processes as have been operative in transforming fetishism and magic into religion and philosophy, or scattered fragm
78.13: ents of knowledge into science. [78] Otis T. Mason: _The Origins of Inventions_. (London, 1902.) Psychologically, invention depe
78.14: nds upon the constructive imagination; that is, upon the ability to abstract from what is immediately present to the senses and
78.15: to picture new situations with their possibilities and consequences. Images are united in order to form new combinations. As we
78.16: have several times emphasized, the decisive intellectual differences among human beings are not greatly dependent upon mere sens
78.17: e discrimination or native retentiveness. Far more important than the raw mass of sense data is the correct shooting together of
78.18: the sense elements in memory and imagination. This is but another name for invention. It is the synthetic, or apperceptive, act
78.19: ivity of the mind that gives the "sevenleague boots" to genius. It is, however, a kind of ability which is possessed by all mind

85.38: r amount of patience and force of will on the part of the reader. The author has spared himself no pains in his endeavour to pre
85.39: sent the main ideas in the simplest and most intelligible form, and on the whole, in the sequence and connection in which they a
85.40: ctually originated. In the interest of clearness, it appeared to me inevitable that I should repeat myself frequently, without p

85.46: suggestive thought! December, 1916 A. EINSTEIN PART I: THE SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY I. PHYSICAL MEANING OF GEOMETRICAL PROPO
85.47: SITIONS In your schooldays most of you who read this book made acquaintance with the noble building of Euclid’s geometry, and yo
85.48: u remember—perhaps with more respect than love—the magnificent structure, on the lofty staircase of which you were chased about
85.49: for uncounted hours by conscientious teachers. By reason of our past experience, you would certainly regard everyone with disdai
85.50: n who should pronounce even the most outoftheway proposition of this science to be untrue. But perhaps this feeling of proud cer
85.51: tainty would leave you immediately if some one were to ask you: “What, then, do you mean by the assertion that these proposition
85.52: s are true?” Let us proceed to give this question a little consideration. Geometry sets out from certain conceptions such as “pl
85.53: ane,” “point,” and “straight line,” with which we are able to associate more or less definite ideas, and from certain simple pro
85.54: positions (axioms) which, in virtue of these ideas, we are inclined to accept as “true.” Then, on the basis of a logical process
85.55: , the justification of which we feel ourselves compelled to admit, all remaining propositions are shown to follow from those axi
85.56: oms, _i.e._ they are proven. A proposition is then correct (“true”) when it has been derived in the recognised manner from the a
85.57: xioms. The question of “truth” of the individual geometrical propositions is thus reduced to one of the “truth” of the axioms. N
85.58: ow it has long been known that the last question is not only unanswerable by the methods of geometry, but that it is in itself e
85.59: ntirely without meaning. We cannot ask whether it is true that only one straight line goes through two points. We can only say t
85.60: hat Euclidean geometry deals with things called “straight lines,” to each of which is ascribed the property of being uniquely de
85.61: termined by two points situated on it. The concept “true” does not tally with the assertions of pure geometry, because by the wo
85.62: rd “true” we are eventually in the habit of designating always the correspondence with a “real” object; geometry, however, is no
85.63: t concerned with the relation of the ideas involved in it to objects of experience, but only with the logical connection of thes
85.64: e ideas among themselves. It is not difficult to understand why, in spite of this, we feel constrained to call the propositions

86.1: of geometry “true.” Geometrical ideas correspond to more or less exact objects in nature, and these last are undoubtedly the exc
86.2: lusive cause of the genesis of those ideas. Geometry ought to refrain from such a course, in order to give to its structure the
86.3: largest possible logical unity. The practice, for example, of seeing in a “distance” two marked positions on a practically rigid
86.4: body is something which is lodged deeply in our habit of thought. We are accustomed further to regard three points as being sit
86.5: uated on a straight line, if their apparent positions can be made to coincide for observation with one eye, under suitable choic
86.6: e of our place of observation. If, in pursuance of our habit of thought, we now supplement the propositions of Euclidean geometr
86.7: y by the single proposition that two points on a practically rigid body always correspond to the same distance (lineinterval), i
86.8: ndependently of any changes in position to which we may subject the body, the propositions of Euclidean geometry then resolve th
86.9: emselves into propositions on the possible relative position of practically rigid bodies.[1] Geometry which has been supplemente
86.10: d in this way is then to be treated as a branch of physics. We can now legitimately ask as to the “truth” of geometrical proposi
86.11: tions interpreted in this way, since we are justified in asking whether these propositions are satisfied for those real things w
86.12: e have associated with the geometrical ideas. In less exact terms we can express this by saying that by the “truth” of a geometr
86.13: ical proposition in this sense we understand its validity for a construction with rule and compasses. [1] It follows that a natu
86.14: ral object is associated also with a straight line. Three points _A, B_ and _C_ on a rigid body thus lie in a straight line when
86.15: the points _A_ and _C_ being given, _B_ is chosen such that the sum of the distances _AB_ and _BC_ is as short as possible. Thi
86.16: s incomplete suggestion will suffice for the present purpose. Of course the conviction of the “truth” of geometrical proposition
86.17: s in this sense is founded exclusively on rather incomplete experience. For the present we shall assume the “truth” of the geome
86.18: trical propositions, then at a later stage (in the general theory of relativity) we shall see that this “truth” is limited, and
86.19: we shall consider the extent of its limitation. II. THE SYSTEM OF COORDINATES On the basis of the physical interpretation of dis
86.20: tance which has been indicated, we are also in a position to establish the distance between two points on a rigid body by means
86.21: of measurements. For this purpose we require a “distance” (rod _S_) which is to be used once and for all, and which we employ as
86.22: a standard measure. If, now, _A_ and _B_ are two points on a rigid body, we can construct the line joining them according to th
86.23: e rules of geometry; then, starting from _A_, we can mark off the distance _S_ time after time until we reach _B_. The number of
86.24: these operations required is the numerical measure of the distance _AB_. This is the basis of all measurement of length.[2] [2]
86.25: Here we have assumed that there is nothing left over _i.e._ that the measurement gives a whole number. This difficulty is got o
86.26: ver by the use of divided measuringrods, the introduction of which does not demand any fundamentally new method. Every descripti
86.27: on of the scene of an event or of the position of an object in space is based on the specification of the point on a rigid body
86.28: (body of reference) with which that event or object coincides. This applies not only to scientific description, but also to ever
86.29: yday life. If I analyse the place specification “Trafalgar Square, London”[3] I arrive at the following result. The earth is the
86.30: rigid body to which the specification of place refers; “Trafalgar Square, London” is a welldefined point, to which a name has b
86.31: een assigned, and with which the event coincides in space.[4] [3] I have chosen this as being more familiar to the English reade
86.32: r than the “Potzdammer Platz, Berlin,” which is referred to in the original. (R. W. L.) [4] It is not necessary here to investig
86.33: ate further the significance of the expression “coincidence in space.” This conception is sufficiently obvious to ensure that di
86.34: fferences of opinion are scarcely likely to arise as to its applicability in practice. This primitive method of place specificat
86.35: ion deals only with places on the surface of rigid bodies, and is dependent on the existence of points on this surface which are
86.36: distinguishable from each other. But we can free ourselves from both of these limitations without altering the nature of our sp
86.37: ecification of position. If, for instance, a cloud is hovering over Trafalgar Square, then we can determine its position relativ
86.38: e to the surface of the earth by erecting a pole perpendicularly on the Square, so that it reaches the cloud. The length of the
86.39: pole measured with the standard measuringrod, combined with the specification of the position of the foot of the pole, supplies
86.40: us with a complete place specification. On the basis of this illustration, we are able to see the manner in which a refinement o
86.41: f the conception of position has been developed. (_a_) We imagine the rigid body, to which the place specification is referred,
86.42: supplemented in such a manner that the object whose position we require is reached by the completed rigid body. (_b_) In locatin
86.43: g the position of the object, we make use of a number (here the length of the pole measured with the measuringrod) instead of de
86.44: signated points of reference. (_c_) We speak of the height of the cloud even when the pole which reaches the cloud has not been
86.45: erected. By means of optical observations of the cloud from different positions on the ground, and taking into account the prope
86.46: rties of the propagation of light, we determine the length of the pole we should have required in order to reach the cloud. From
86.47: this consideration we see that it will be advantageous if, in the description of position, it should be possible by means of nu
86.48: merical measures to make ourselves independent of the existence of marked positions (possessing names) on the rigid body of refe
86.49: rence. In the physics of measurement this is attained by the application of the Cartesian system of coordinates. This consists o
86.50: f three plane surfaces perpendicular to each other and rigidly attached to a rigid body. Referred to a system of coordinates, th
86.51: e scene of any event will be determined (for the main part) by the specification of the lengths of the three perpendiculars or c
86.52: oordinates (_x, y, z_) which can be dropped from the scene of the event to those three plane surfaces. The lengths of these thre
86.53: e perpendiculars can be determined by a series of manipulations with rigid measuringrods performed according to the rules and me
86.54: thods laid down by Euclidean geometry. In practice, the rigid surfaces which constitute the system of coordinates are generally
86.55: not available; furthermore, the magnitudes of the coordinates are not actually determined by constructions with rigid rods, but
86.56: by indirect means. If the results of physics and astronomy are to maintain their clearness, the physical meaning of specificatio
86.57: ns of position must always be sought in accordance with the above considerations.[5] [5] A refinement and modification of these
86.58: views does not become necessary until we come to deal with the general theory of relativity, treated in the second part of this
86.59: book. We thus obtain the following result: Every description of events in space involves the use of a rigid body to which such e
86.60: vents have to be referred. The resulting relationship takes for granted that the laws of Euclidean geometry hold for “distances;
86.61: ” the “distance” being represented physically by means of the convention of two marks on a rigid body. III. SPACE AND TIME IN CL
86.62: ASSICAL MECHANICS The purpose of mechanics is to describe how bodies change their position in space with “time.” I should load m
86.63: y conscience with grave sins against the sacred spirit of lucidity were I to formulate the aims of mechanics in this way, withou
86.64: t serious reflection and detailed explanations. Let us proceed to disclose these sins. It is not clear what is to be understood

87.1: here by “position” and “space.” I stand at the window of a railway carriage which is travelling uniformly, and drop a stone on t
87.2: he embankment, without throwing it. Then, disregarding the influence of the air resistance, I see the stone descend in a straigh
87.3: t line. A pedestrian who observes the misdeed from the footpath notices that the stone falls to earth in a parabolic curve. I no
87.4: w ask: Do the “positions” traversed by the stone lie “in reality” on a straight line or on a parabola? Moreover, what is meant h
87.5: ere by motion “in space”? From the considerations of the previous section the answer is selfevident. In the first place we entir
87.6: ely shun the vague word “space,” of which, we must honestly acknowledge, we cannot form the slightest conception, and we replace
87.7: it by “motion relative to a practically rigid body of reference.” The positions relative to the body of reference (railway carr
87.8: iage or embankment) have already been defined in detail in the preceding section. If instead of “body of reference” we insert “s
87.9: ystem of coordinates,” which is a useful idea for mathematical description, we are in a position to say: The stone traverses a s
87.10: traight line relative to a system of coordinates rigidly attached to the carriage, but relative to a system of coordinates rigid
87.11: ly attached to the ground (embankment) it describes a parabola. With the aid of this example it is clearly seen that there is no
87.12: such thing as an independently existing trajectory (lit. “pathcurve”[6], but only a trajectory relative to a particular body of
87.13: reference. [6] That is, a curve along which the body moves. In order to have a _complete_ description of the motion, we must sp
87.14: ecify how the body alters its position _with time; i.e._ for every point on the trajectory it must be stated at what time the bo
87.15: dy is situated there. These data must be supplemented by such a definition of time that, in virtue of this definition, these tim
87.16: evalues can be regarded essentially as magnitudes (results of measurements) capable of observation. If we take our stand on the
87.17: ground of classical mechanics, we can satisfy this requirement for our illustration in the following manner. We imagine two cloc
87.18: ks of identical construction; the man at the railwaycarriage window is holding one of them, and the man on the footpath the othe
87.19: r. Each of the observers determines the position on his own referencebody occupied by the stone at each tick of the clock he is
87.20: holding in his hand. In this connection we have not taken account of the inaccuracy involved by the finiteness of the velocity o
87.21: f propagation of light. With this and with a second difficulty prevailing here we shall have to deal in detail later. IV. THE GA
87.22: LILEIAN SYSTEM OF COORDINATES As is well known, the fundamental law of the mechanics of GalileiNewton, which is known as the _la
87.23: w of inertia_, can be stated thus: A body removed sufficiently far from other bodies continues in a state of rest or of uniform
87.24: motion in a straight line. This law not only says something about the motion of the bodies, but it also indicates the referenceb
87.25: odies or systems of coordinates, permissible in mechanics, which can be used in mechanical description. The visible fixed stars
87.26: are bodies for which the law of inertia certainly holds to a high degree of approximation. Now if we use a system of coordinates
87.27: which is rigidly attached to the earth, then, relative to this system, every fixed star describes a circle of immense radius in
87.28: the course of an astronomical day, a result which is opposed to the statement of the law of inertia. So that if we adhere to th
87.29: is law we must refer these motions only to systems of coordinates relative to which the fixed stars do not move in a circle. A s
87.30: ystem of coordinates of which the state of motion is such that the law of inertia holds relative to it is called a “Galileian sy
87.31: stem of coordinates.” The laws of the mechanics of GalileiNewton can be regarded as valid only for a Galileian system of coordin
87.32: ates. V. THE PRINCIPLE OF RELATIVITY (IN THE RESTRICTED SENSE) In order to attain the greatest possible clearness, let us return
87.33: to our example of the railway carriage supposed to be travelling uniformly. We call its motion a uniform translation (“uniform”
87.34: because it is of constant velocity and direction, “translation” because although the carriage changes its position relative to
87.35: the embankment yet it does not rotate in so doing). Let us imagine a raven flying through the air in such a manner that its moti
87.36: on, as observed from the embankment, is uniform and in a straight line. If we were to observe the flying raven from the moving r
87.37: ailway carriage. we should find that the motion of the raven would be one of different velocity and direction, but that it would
87.38: still be uniform and in a straight line. Expressed in an abstract manner we may say: If a mass _m_ is moving uniformly in a str
87.39: aight line with respect to a coordinate system _K_, then it will also be moving uniformly and in a straight line relative to a s
87.40: econd coordinate system _K′_ provided that the latter is executing a uniform translatory motion with respect to _K_. In accordan
87.41: ce with the discussion contained in the preceding section, it follows that: If _K_ is a Galileian coordinate system. then every
87.42: other coordinate system _K′_ is a Galileian one, when, in relation to _K_, it is in a condition of uniform motion of translation
87.43: . Relative to _K′_ the mechanical laws of GalileiNewton hold good exactly as they do with respect to _K_. We advance a step fart
87.44: her in our generalisation when we express the tenet thus: If, relative to _K_, _K′_ is a uniformly moving coordinate system devo
87.45: id of rotation, then natural phenomena run their course with respect to _K′_ according to exactly the same general laws as with
87.46: respect to _K_. This statement is called the _principle of relativity_ (in the restricted sense). As long as one was convinced t
87.47: hat all natural phenomena were capable of representation with the help of classical mechanics, there was no need to doubt the va
87.48: lidity of this principle of relativity. But in view of the more recent development of electrodynamics and optics it became more
87.49: and more evident that classical mechanics affords an insufficient foundation for the physical description of all natural phenome
87.50: na. At this juncture the question of the validity of the principle of relativity became ripe for discussion, and it did not appe
87.51: ar impossible that the answer to this question might be in the negative. Nevertheless, there are two general facts which at the
87.52: outset speak very much in favour of the validity of the principle of relativity. Even though classical mechanics does not supply
87.53: us with a sufficiently broad basis for the theoretical presentation of all physical phenomena, still we must grant it a conside
87.54: rable measure of “truth,” since it supplies us with the actual motions of the heavenly bodies with a delicacy of detail little s
87.55: hort of wonderful. The principle of relativity must therefore apply with great accuracy in the domain of _mechanics_. But that a
87.56: principle of such broad generality should hold with such exactness in one domain of phenomena, and yet should be invalid for an
87.57: other, is _a priori_ not very probable. We now proceed to the second argument, to which, moreover, we shall return later. If the
87.58: principle of relativity (in the restricted sense) does not hold, then the Galileian coordinate systems _K, K′, K″_, etc., which
87.59: are moving uniformly relative to each other, will not be _equivalent_ for the description of natural phenomena. In this case we
87.60: should be constrained to believe that natural laws are capable of being formulated in a particularly simple manner, and of cour
87.61: se only on condition that, from amongst all possible Galileian coordinate systems, we should have chosen _one_ (_K0_) of a parti
87.62: cular state of motion as our body of reference. We should then be justified (because of its merits for the description of natura
87.63: l phenomena) in calling this system “absolutely at rest,” and all other Galileian systems _K_ “in motion.” If, for instance, our
87.64: embankment were the system _K0_ then our railway carriage would be a system _K_, relative to which less simple laws would hold

88.1: than with respect to _K0_. This diminished simplicity would be due to the fact that the carriage _K_ would be in motion (_i.e._
88.2: “really”)with respect to _K0_. In the general laws of nature which have been formulated with reference to _K_, the magnitude and
88.3: direction of the velocity of the carriage would necessarily play a part. We should expect, for instance, that the note emitted
88.4: by an organpipe placed with its axis parallel to the direction of travel would be different from that emitted if the axis of the
88.5: pipe were placed perpendicular to this direction. Now in virtue of its motion in an orbit round the sun, our earth is comparabl
88.6: e with a railway carriage travelling with a velocity of about 30 kilometres per second. If the principle of relativity were not
88.7: valid we should therefore expect that the direction of motion of the earth at any moment would enter into the laws of nature, an
88.8: d also that physical systems in their behaviour would be dependent on the orientation in space with respect to the earth. For ow
88.9: ing to the alteration in direction of the velocity of revolution of the earth in the course of a year, the earth cannot be at re
88.10: st relative to the hypothetical system _K0_ throughout the whole year. However, the most careful observations have never reveale
88.11: d such anisotropic properties in terrestrial physical space, _i.e._ a physical nonequivalence of different directions. This is v
88.12: ery powerful argument in favour of the principle of relativity. VI. THE THEOREM OF THE ADDITION OF VELOCITIES EMPLOYED IN CLASSI
88.13: CAL MECHANICS Let us suppose our old friend the railway carriage to be travelling along the rails with a constant velocity _v_,
88.14: and that a man traverses the length of the carriage in the direction of travel with a velocity _w_. How quickly or, in other wor
88.15: ds, with what velocity _W_ does the man advance relative to the embankment during the process? The only possible answer seems to
88.16: result from the following consideration: If the man were to stand still for a second, he would advance relative to the embankme
88.17: nt through a distance _v_ equal numerically to the velocity of the carriage. As a consequence of his walking, however, he traver
88.18: ses an additional distance w relative to the carriage, and hence also relative to the embankment, in this second, the distance w
88.19: being numerically equal to the velocity with which he is walking. Thus in total he covers the distance _W = v + w_ relative to
88.20: the embankment in the second considered. We shall see later that this result, which expresses the theorem of the addition of vel
88.21: ocities employed in classical mechanics, cannot be maintained; in other words, the law that we have just written down does not h
88.22: old in reality. For the time being, however, we shall assume its correctness. VII. THE APPARENT INCOMPATIBILITY OF THE LAW OF PR
88.23: OPAGATION OF LIGHT WITH THE PRINCIPLE OF RELATIVITY There is hardly a simpler law in physics than that according to which light
88.24: is propagated in empty space. Every child at school knows, or believes he knows, that this propagation takes place in straight l
88.25: ines with a velocity _c_ = 300,000 km./sec. At all events we know with great exactness that this velocity is the same for all co
88.26: lours, because if this were not the case, the minimum of emission would not be observed simultaneously for different colours dur
88.27: ing the eclipse of a fixed star by its dark neighbour. By means of similar considerations based on observations of double stars,
88.28: the Dutch astronomer De Sitter was also able to show that the velocity of propagation of light cannot depend on the velocity of
88.29: motion of the body emitting the light. The assumption that this velocity of propagation is dependent on the direction “in space
88.30: ” is in itself improbable. In short, let us assume that the simple law of the constancy of the velocity of light _c_ (in vacuum)
88.31: is justifiably believed by the child at school. Who would imagine that this simple law has plunged the conscientiously thoughtf
88.32: ul physicist into the greatest intellectual difficulties? Let us consider how these difficulties arise. Of course we must refer

88.34: system let us again choose our embankment. We shall imagine the air above it to have been removed. If a ray of light be sent al
88.35: ong the embankment, we see from the above that the tip of the ray will be transmitted with the velocity _c_ relative to the emba
88.36: nkment. Now let us suppose that our railway carriage is again travelling along the railway lines with the velocity _v_, and that

127.37: 279 THE MEASUREMENT OF INTELLIGENCE PART I PROBLEMS AND RESULTS THE MEASUREMENT OF INTELLIGENCE CHAPTER I THE USES OF
127.38: INTELLIGENCE TESTS INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF RETARDED SCHOOL CHILDREN. Numerous studies of the agegrade progress of school children
127.39: have afforded convincing evidence of the magnitude and seriousness of the retardation problem. Statistics collected in hundreds
127.40: of cities in the United States show that between a third and a half of the school children fail to progress through the grades
127.41: at the expected rate; that from 10 to 15 per cent are retarded two years or more; and that from 5 to 8 per cent are retarded at
127.42: least three years. More than 10 per cent of the $400,000,000 annually expended in the United States for school instruction is de
127.43: voted to reteaching children what they have already been taught but have failed to learn. The first efforts at reform which resu
127.44: lted from these findings were based on the supposition that the evils which had been discovered could be remedied by the individ
127.45: ualizing of instruction, by improved methods of promotion, by increased attention to children's health, and by other reforms in
127.46: school administration. Although reforms along these lines have been productive of much good, they have nevertheless been in a me
127.47: asure disappointing. The trouble was, they were too often based upon the assumption that under the right conditions all children
127.48: would be equally, or almost equally, capable of making satisfactory school progress. Psychological studies of school children b
127.49: y means of standardized intelligence tests have shown that this supposition is not in accord with the facts. It has been found t
127.50: hat children do not fall into two welldefined groups, the "feebleminded" and the "normal." Instead, there are many grades of int
127.51: elligence, ranging from idiocy on the one hand to genius on the other. Among those classed as normal, vast individual difference
127.52: s have been found to exist in original mental endowment, differences which affect profoundly the capacity to profit from school
127.53: instruction. We are beginning to realize that the school must take into account, more seriously than it has yet done, the existe
127.54: nce and significance of these differences in endowment. Instead of wasting energy in the vain attempt to hold mentally slow and
127.55: defective children up to a level of progress which is normal to the average child, it will be wiser to take account of the inequ
127.56: alities of children in original endowment and to differentiate the course of study in such a way that each child will be allowed
127.57: to progress at the rate which is normal to him, whether that rate be rapid or slow. While we cannot hold all children to the sa
127.58: me standard of school progress, we can at least prevent the kind of retardation which involves failure and the repetition of a s
127.59: chool grade. It is well enough recognized that children do not enter with very much zest upon school work in which they have onc
127.60: e failed. Failure crushes selfconfidence and destroys the spirit of work. It is a sad fact that a large proportion of children i
127.61: n the schools are acquiring the habit of failure. The remedy, of course, is to measure out the work for each child in proportion
127.62: to his mental ability. Before an engineer constructs a railroad bridge or trestle, he studies the materials to be used, and lea
127.63: rns by means of tests exactly the amount of strain per unit of size his materials will be able to withstand. He does not work em
127.64: pirically, and count upon patching up the mistakes which may later appear under the stress of actual use. The educational engine

128.1: er should emulate this example. Tests and forethought must take the place of failure and patchwork. Our efforts have been too lo
128.2: ng directed by "trial and error." It is time to leave off guessing and to acquire a scientific knowledge of the material with wh
128.3: ich we have to deal. When instruction must be repeated, it means that the school, as well as the pupil, has failed. Every child
128.4: who fails in his school work or is in danger of failing should be given a mental examination. The examination takes less than on
128.5: e hour, and the result will contribute more to a real understanding of the case than anything else that could be done. It is nec
128.6: essary to determine whether a given child is unsuccessful in school because of poor native ability, or because of poor instructi
128.7: on, lack of interest, or some other removable cause. It is not sufficient to establish any number of special classes, if they ar
128.8: e to be made the dumpingground for all kinds of troublesome casesthe feebleminded, the physically defective, the merely backward
128.9: , the truants, the incorrigibles, etc. Without scientific diagnosis and classification of these children the educational work of
128.10: the special class must blunder along in the dark. In such diagnosis and classification our main reliance must always be in ment
128.11: al tests, properly used and properly interpreted. INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF THE FEEBLEMINDED. Thus far intelligence tests have found
128.12: their chief application in the identification and grading of the feebleminded. Their value for this purpose is twofold. In the
128.13: first place, it is necessary to ascertain the degree of defect before it is possible to decide intelligently upon either the con
128.14: tent or the method of instruction suited to the training of the backward child. In the second place, intelligence tests are rapi
128.15: dly extending our conception of "feeblemindedness" to include milder degrees of defect than have generally been associated with
128.16: this term. The earlier methods of diagnosis caused a majority of the higher grade defectives to be overlooked. Previous to the d
128.17: evelopment of psychological methods the lowgrade moron was about as high a type of defective as most physicians or even psycholo
128.18: gists were able to identify as feebleminded. Wherever intelligence tests have been made in any considerable number in the school
128.19: s, they have shown that not far from 2 per cent of the children enrolled have a grade of intelligence which, however long they l
128.20: ive, will never develop beyond the level which is normal to the average child of 11 or 12 years. The large majority of these bel
128.21: ong to the moron grade; that is, their mental development will stop somewhere between the 7year and 12year level of intelligence
128.22: , more often between 9 and 12. The more we learn about such children, the clearer it becomes that they must be looked upon as re
128.23: al defectives. They may be able to drag along to the fourth, fifth, or sixth grades, but even by the age of 16 or 18 years they
128.24: are never able to cope successfully with the more abstract and difficult parts of the commonschool course of study. They may mas
128.25: ter a certain amount of rote learning, such as that involved in reading and in the manipulation of number combinations but they
128.26: cannot be taught to meet new conditions effectively or to think, reason, and judge as normal persons do. It is safe to predict t
128.27: hat in the near future intelligence tests will bring tens of thousands of these highgrade defectives under the surveillance and
128.28: protection of society. This will ultimately result in curtailing the reproduction of feeblemindedness and in the elimination of
128.29: an enormous amount of crime, pauperism, and industrial inefficiency. It is hardly necessary to emphasize that the highgrade case
128.30: s, of the type now so frequently overlooked, are precisely the ones whose guardianship it is most important for the State to ass
128.31: ume. INTELLIGENCE TESTS OF DELINQUENTS. One of the most important facts brought to light by the use of intelligence tests is the
128.32: frequent association of delinquency and mental deficiency. Although it has long been recognized that the proportion of feeblemi
128.33: ndedness among offenders is rather large, the real amount has, until recently, been underestimated even by the most competent st
128.34: udents of criminology. The criminologists have been accustomed to give more attention to the physical than to the mental correla
128.35: tes of crime. Thus, Lombroso and his followers subjected thousands of criminals to observation and measurement with regard to su
128.36: ch physical traits as size and shape of the skull, bilateral asymmetries, anomalies of the ear, eye, nose, palate, teeth, hands,
128.37: fingers, hair, dermal sensitivity, etc. The search was for physical "stigmata" characteristic of the "criminal type." Although
128.38: such studies performed an important service in creating a scientific interest in criminology, the theories of Lombroso have been
128.39: wholly discredited by the results of intelligence tests. Such tests have demonstrated, beyond any possibility of doubt, that th
128.40: e most important trait of at least 25 per cent of our criminals is mental weakness. The physical abnormalities which have been f
128.41: ound so common among prisoners are not the stigmata of criminality, but the physical accompaniments of feeblemindedness. They ha
128.42: ve no diagnostic significance except in so far as they are indications of mental deficiency. Without exception, every study whic
128.43: h has been made of the intelligence level of delinquents has furnished convincing testimony as to the close relation existing be
128.44: tween mental weakness and moral abnormality. Some of these findings are as follows: Miss Renz tested 100 girls of the Ohio State
128.45: Reformatory and reported 36 per cent as certainly feebleminded. In every one of these cases the commitment papers had given the

128.48: another of 15½ had 8year intelligence. Of 56 delinquent girls 14 to 20 years of age tested by Hill and Goddard, almost half belo

130.57: the work of the next higher grade. The brief intelligence test is not only more enlightening than the examination; it is also m
