133.36: There was a very general tendency to judge intelligence by success in one or more of the school studies. Some thought that abil
133.37: ity to master arithmetic was a sure criterion. Others were influenced almost entirely by the pupil's ability to read. One teache
133.38: r said that the child who can "read so expressively as to make you feel the punctuation" is certainly intelligent, an observatio
133.39: n which is rather good, as far as it goes. A few judged intelligence by the pupil's knowledge of such subjects as history and ge
133.40: ography, which, as Binet points out, is to confound intelligence with the ability to memorize. "Memory," says Binet, is a "great
133.41: simulator of intelligence." It is a wise teacher who is not deceived by it. Only a small minority mentioned resourcefulness in
133.42: play, capacity to adjust to practical situations, or any other outofschool criteria. Some suggested asking the pupil such questi
133.43: ons as the following: "Why do you love your parents?" "If it takes three persons seven hours to do a piece of work, would it tak
133.44: e seven persons any longer?" "Which would you rather have, a fourth of a pie, or a half of a half?" "Which is heavier, a pound o
133.45: f feathers or a pound of lead?" "If you had twenty cents what would you do with it?" A great many based their judgment mainly on
133.46: the general appearance of the face and eyes. An "active" or "passive" expression of the eyes was looked upon as especially sign
133.47: ificant. One teacher thought that a mere "glance of the eye" was sufficient to display the grade of intelligence. If the eyes ar
133.48: e penetrating, reflective, or show curiosity, the child must be intelligent; if they are heavy and expressionless, he must be du
133.49: ll. The mobility of countenance came in for frequent mention, also the shape of the head. No one will deny that intelligence dis
133.50: plays itself to a greater or less extent in the features; but how, asks Binet, are we going to _standardize_ a "glance of the ey
133.51: e" or an "expression of curiosity" so that it will serve as an exact measure of intelligence? The fact is, the more one sees of
133.52: feebleminded children, the less reliance one comes to place upon facial expression as a sign of intelligence. Some children who
133.53: are only slightly backward have the general appearance of lowgrade imbeciles. On the other hand, not a few who are distinctly fe
133.54: ebleminded are pretty and attractive. With many such children a ready smile takes the place of comprehension. If the smile is ra
133.55: ther sweet and sympathetic, as is often the case, the observer is almost sure to be deceived. As regards the shape of the head,
133.56: peculiar conformation of the ears, and other "stigmata," science long ago demonstrated that these are ordinarily of little or no
133.57: significance. In reply to the second question, some teachers stated that they never made a mistake, while others admitted failu
133.58: re in one case out of three. Still others said, "Once in ten years," "once in twenty years," "once in a thousand times," etc. As
133.59: Binet remarks, the answers to this question are not very enlightening. In the first place, the teacher as a rule loses sight of
133.60: the pupil when he has passed from her care, and seldom has opportunity of finding out whether his later success belies her judg
133.61: ment or confirms it. Errors go undiscovered for the simple reason that there is no opportunity to check them up. In the second p
133.62: lace, her estimate is so rough that an error must be very great in order to have any meaning. If I say that a man is six feet an
133.63: d two inches tall, it is easy enough to apply a measuring stick and prove the correctness or incorrectness of my assertion. But
133.64: if I say simply that the man is "rather tall," or "very tall," the error must be very extreme before we can expose it, particula

134.1: rly since the estimate can itself be checked up only by observation and not by controlled experiment. The teachers' answers seem
134.2: to justify three conclusions: 1. Teachers do not have a very definite idea of what constitutes intelligence. They tend to confu
134.3: se it variously with capacity for memorizing, facility in reading, ability to master arithmetic, etc. On the whole, their standa
134.4: rd is too academic. They fail to appreciate the onesidedness of the school's demands upon intelligence. In a quaintly humorous p
134.5: assage discussing this tendency, Binet characterizes the child in a class as _dénaturé_, a French word which we may translate (t
134.6: hough rather too literally) as "denatured." Too often this "denatured" child of the classroom is the only child the teacher know
134.7: s. 2. In judging intelligence teachers are too easily deceived by a sprightly attitude, a sympathetic expression, a glance of th
134.8: e eye, or a chance "bump" on the head. 3. Although a few teachers seem to realize the many possibilities of error, the majority
134.9: show rather undue confidence in the accuracy of their judgment. BINET'S EXPERIMENT ON HOW TEACHERS TEST INTELLIGENCE.[9] Finally
134.10: , Binet had three teachers come to his laboratory to judge the intelligence of children whom they had never seen before. Each sp
134.11: ent an afternoon in the laboratory and examined five pupils. In each case the teacher was left free to arrive at a conclusion in
134.12: her own way. Binet, who remained in the room and took notes, recounts with playful humor how the teachers were unavoidably comp
134.13: elled to resort to the muchabused test method, although their attempts at using it were sometimes, from the psychologist's point
134.14: of view, amusingly clumsy. [9] See p. 182 _ff._ of reference 2 at end of this book. One teacher, for example, questioned the ch
134.15: ildren about some canals and sluices which were in the vicinity, asking what their purpose was and how they worked. Another show
134.16: ed the children some pretty pictures, which she had brought with her for the purpose, and asked questions about them. Showing th
134.17: e picture of a garret, she asked how a garret differs from an ordinary room. One teacher asked whether in building a factory it
134.18: was best to have the walls thick or thin. As King Edward had just died, another teacher questioned the children about the detail
134.19: s of this event, in order to find out whether they were in the habit of reading the newspapers, or understood the things they he
134.20: ard others read. Other questions related to the names of the streets in the neighborhood, the road one should take to reach a ce
134.21: rtain point in the vicinity, etc. Binet notes that many of the questions were special, and were only applicable with the childre
134.22: n of this particular school. The method of proposing the questions and judging the responses was also at fault. The teachers did
134.23: not adhere consistently to any definite formula in giving a particular test to the different children. Instead, the questions w
134.24: ere materially altered from time to time. One teacher scored the identical response differently for two children, giving one chi
134.25: ld more credit than the other because she had already judged his intelligence to be superior. In several cases the examination w
134.26: as needlessly delayed in order to instruct the child in what he did not know. The examination ended, quite properly for a teache
134.27: r's examination, with questions about history, literature, the metric system, etc., and with the recitation of a fable. A compar
134.28: ison of the results showed hardly any agreement among the estimates of the three teachers. When questioned about the standard th
134.29: at had been taken in arriving at their conclusions, one teacher said she had taken the answers of the first pupil as a point of
134.30: departure, and that she had judged the other pupils by this one. Another judged all the children by a child of her acquaintance
134.31: whom she knew to be intelligent. This was, of course, an unsafe method, because no one could say how the child taken as an ideal
134.32: would have responded to the tests used with the five children. In summarizing the result of his little experiment, Binet points
134.33: out that the teachers employed, as if by instinct, the very method which he himself recommends. In using it, however, they made
134.34: numerous errors. Their questions were often needlessly long. Several were "dilemma questions," that is, answerable by _yes_ or
134.35: _no_. In such cases chance alone will cause fifty per cent of the answers to be correct. Some of the questions were merely tests
134.36: of school knowledge. Others were entirely special, usable only with the children of this particular school on this particular d
134.37: ay. Not all of the questions were put in the same terms, and a given response did not always receive the same score. When the ch
134.38: ildren responded incorrectly or incompletely, they were often given help, but not always to the same extent. In other words, say
134.39: s Binet, it was evident that "the teachers employed very awkwardly a very excellent method." The above remark is as pertinent as
134.40: it is expressive. As the statement implies, the test method is but a refinement and standardization of the commonsense approach
134.41: . Binet remarks that most people who inquire into his method of measuring intelligence do so expecting to find something very su
134.42: rprising and mysterious; and on seeing how much it resembles the methods which common sense employs in ordinary life, they heave
134.43: a sigh of disappointment and say, "Is that all?" Binet reminds us that the difference between the scientific and unscientific w
134.44: ay of doing a thing is not necessarily a difference in the _nature_ of the method; it is often merely a difference in _exactness
134.45: _. Science does the thing better, because it does it more accurately. It was of course not the purpose of Binet to cast a slur u
134.46: pon the good sense and judgment of teachers. The teachers who took part in the little experiment described above were Binet's pe
134.47: rsonal friends. The errors he points out in his entertaining and goodhumored account of the experiment are inherent in the situa
134.48: tion. They are the kind of errors which any person, however discriminating and observant, is likely to make in estimating the in
134.49: telligence of a subject without the use of standardized tests. It is the writer's experience that the teacher's estimate of a ch
134.50: ild's intelligence is much more reliable than that of the average parent; more accurate even than that of the physician who has
134.51: not had psychological training. Indeed, it is an exceptional school physician who is able to give any very valuable assistance t
134.52: o teachers in the classification of mentally exceptional children for special pedagogical treatment. This is only to be expected
134.53: , for the physician has ordinarily had much less instruction in psychology than the teacher, and of course infinitely less exper
134.54: ience in judging the mental performances of children. Even if graduated from a firstrank medical school, the instruction he has
134.55: received in the important subject of mental deficiency has probably been less adequate than that given to the students of a stan
134.56: dard normal school. As a rule, the doctor has no equipment or special fitness which gives him any advantage over the teacher in
134.57: acquiring facility in the use of intelligence tests. As for parents, it would of course be unreasonable to expect from them a ve
134.58: ry accurate judgment regarding the mental peculiarities of their children. The difficulty is not simply that which comes from la
134.59: ck of special training. The presence of parental affection renders impartial judgment impossible. Still more serious are the eff
134.60: ects of habituation to the child's mental traits. As a result of such habituation the most intelligent parent tends to develop a
134.61: n unfortunate blindness to all sorts of abnormalities which exist in his own children. The only way of escape from the fallacies
134.62: we have mentioned lies in the use of some kind of refined psychological procedure. Binet testing is destined to become universa
134.63: lly known and practiced in schools, prisons, reformatories, charity stations, orphan asylums, and even ordinary homes, for the s
134.64: ame reason that Babcock testing has become universal in dairying. Each is indispensable to its purpose. CHAPTER III DESCRIPTION

135.1: OF THE BINETSIMON METHOD ESSENTIAL NATURE OF THE SCALE. The Binet scale is made up of an extended series of tests in the nature
135.2: of "stunts," or problems, success in which demands the exercise of intelligence. As left by Binet, the scale consists of 54 test
135.3: s, so graded in difficulty that the easiest lie well within the range of normal 3yearold children, while the hardest tax the int
135.4: elligence of the average adult. The problems are designed primarily to test native intelligence, not school knowledge or home tr
135.5: aining. They try to answer the question "How intelligent is this child?" How much the child has learned is of significance only
135.6: in so far as it throws light on his ability to learn more. Binet fully appreciated the fact that intelligence is not homogeneous
135.7: , that it has many aspects, and that no one kind of test will display it adequately. He therefore assembled for his intelligence
135.8: scale tests of many different types, some of them designed to display differences of memory, others differences in power to rea
135.9: son, ability to compare, power of comprehension, time orientation, facility in the use of number concepts, power to combine idea
135.10: s into a meaningful whole, the maturity of apperception, wealth of ideas, knowledge of common objects, etc. HOW THE SCALE WAS DE
135.11: RIVED. The tests were arranged in order of difficulty, as found by trying them upon some 200 normal children of different ages f
135.12: rom 3 to 15 years. It was found, for illustration, that a certain test was passed by only a very small proportion of the younger
135.13: children, say the 5yearolds, and that the number passing this test increased rapidly in the succeeding years until by the age o
135.14: f 7 or 8 years, let us say, practically all the children were successful. If, in our supposed case, the test was passed by about
135.15: two thirds to three fourths of the normal children aged 7 years, it was considered by Binet a test of 7year intelligence. In li
135.16: ke manner, a test passed by 65 to 75 per cent of the normal 9yearolds was considered a test of 9year intelligence, and so on. By
135.17: trying out many different tests in this way it was possible to secure five tests to represent each age from 3 to 10 years (exce
135.18: pting age 4, which has only four tests), five for age 12, five for 15, and five for adults, making 54 tests in all. LIST OF TEST
135.19: S. The following is the list of tests as arranged by Binet in 1911, shortly before his untimely death: _Age 3:_ 1. Points to nos
135.20: e, eyes, and mouth. 2. Repeats two digits. 3. Enumerates objects in a picture. 4. Gives family name. 5. Repeats a sentence of si
135.21: x syllables. _Age 4:_ 1. Gives his sex. 2. Names key, knife, and penny. 3. Repeats three digits. 4. Compares two lines. _Age 5:_
135.22: 1. Compares two weights. 2. Copies a square. 3. Repeats a sentence of ten syllables. 4. Counts four pennies. 5. Unites the halv
135.23: es of a divided rectangle. _Age 6:_ 1. Distinguishes between morning and afternoon. 2. Defines familiar words in terms of use. 3
135.24: . Copies a diamond. 4. Counts thirteen pennies. 5. Distinguishes pictures of ugly and pretty faces. _Age 7:_ 1. Shows right hand
135.25: and left ear. 2. Describes a picture. 3. Executes three commissions, given simultaneously. 4. Counts the value of six sous, thr
135.26: ee of which are double. 5. Names four cardinal colors. _Age 8:_ 1. Compares two objects from memory. 2. Counts from 20 to 0. 3.
135.27: Notes omissions from pictures. 4. Gives day and date. 5. Repeats five digits. _Age 9:_ 1. Gives change from twenty sous. 2. Defi
135.28: nes familiar words in terms superior to use. 3. Recognizes all the pieces of money. 4. Names the months of the year, in order. 5
135.29: . Answers easy "comprehension questions." _Age 10:_ 1. Arranges five blocks in order of weight. 2. Copies drawings from memory.
135.30: 3. Criticizes absurd statements. 4. Answers difficult "comprehension questions." 5. Uses three given words in not more than two
135.31: sentences. _Age 12:_ 1. Resists suggestion. 2. Composes one sentence containing three given words. 3. Names sixty words in three
135.32: minutes. 4. Defines certain abstract words. 5. Discovers the sense of a disarranged sentence. _Age 15:_ 1. Repeats seven digits
135.33: . 2. Finds three rhymes for a given word. 3. Repeats a sentence of twentysix syllables. 4. Interprets pictures. 5. Interprets gi
135.34: ven facts. _Adult:_ 1. Solves the papercutting test. 2. Rearranges a triangle in imagination. 3. Gives differences between pairs
135.35: of abstract terms. 4. Gives three differences between a president and a king. 5. Gives the main thought of a selection which he
135.36: has heard read. It should be emphasized that merely to name the tests in this way gives little idea of their nature and meaning
135.37: , and tells nothing about Binet's method of conducting the 54 experiments. In order to use the tests intelligently it is necessa
135.38: ry to acquaint one's self thoroughly with the purpose of each test, its correct procedure, and the psychological interpretation
135.39: of different types of response.[10] [10] See Part II of this volume, and References 1 and 29, for discussion and interpretation
135.40: of the individual tests. In fairness to Binet, it should also be borne in mind that the scale of tests was only a rough approxim
135.41: ation to the ideal which the author had set himself to realize. Had his life been spared a few years longer, he would doubtless
135.42: have carried the method much nearer perfection. HOW THE SCALE IS USED. By means of the Binet tests we can judge the intelligence
135.43: of a given individual by comparison with standards of intellectual performance for normal children of different ages. In order
135.44: to make the comparison it is only necessary to begin the examination of the subject at a point in the scale where all the tests
135.45: are passed successfully, and to continue up the scale until no more successes are possible. Then we compare our subject's perfor
135.46: mances with the standard for normal children of the same age, and note the amount of acceleration or retardation. Let us suppose
135.47: the subject being tested is 9 years of age. If he goes as far in the tests as normal 9yearold children ordinarily go, we can sa
135.48: y that the child has a "mental age" of 9 years, which in this case is normal (our child being 9 years of age). If he goes only a
135.49: s far as normal 8yearold children ordinarily go, we say that his "mental age" is 8 years. In like manner, a mentally defective c
135.50: hild of 9 years may have a "mental age" of only 4 years, or a young genius of 9 years may have a mental age of 12 or 13 years. S
135.51: PECIAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE BINETSIMON METHOD. Psychologists had experimented with intelligence tests for at least twenty year
135.52: s before the Binet scale made its appearance. The question naturally suggests itself why Binet should have been successful in a
135.53: field where previous efforts had been for the most part futile. The answer to this question is found in three essential differen
135.54: ces between Binet's method and those formerly employed. 1. _The use of age standards._ Binet was the first to utilize the idea o
135.55: f age standards, or norms, in the measurement of intelligence. It will be understood, of course, that Binet did not set out to i
135.56: nvent tests of 10year intelligence, 6year intelligence, etc. Instead, as already explained, he began with a series of tests rang
135.57: ing from very easy to very difficult, and by trying these tests on children of different ages and noting the percentages of succ
135.58: esses in the various years, he was able to locate them (approximately) in the years where they belonged. This plan has the great
135.59: advantage of giving us standards which are easily grasped. To say, for illustration, that a given subject has a grade of intell
135.60: igence equal to that of the average child of 8 years is a statement whose general import does not need to be explained. Previous
135.61: investigators had worked with subjects the degree of whose intelligence was unknown, and with tests the difficulty of which was
135.62: equally unknown. An immense amount of ingenuity was spent in devising tests which were used in such a way as to preclude any ve
135.63: ry meaningful interpretation of the responses. The Binet method enables us to characterize the intelligence of a child in a far
135.64: more definite way than had hitherto been possible. Current descriptive terms like "bright," "moderately bright," "dull," "very d

136.1: ull," "feebleminded," etc., have had no universally accepted meaning. A child who is designated by one person as "moderately bri
136.2: ght" may be called "very bright" by another person. The degree of intelligence which one calls "moderate dullness," another may
136.3: call "extreme dullness," etc. But every one knows what is meant by the term 8year mentality, 4year mentality, etc., even if he i
136.4: s not able to define these grades of intelligence in psychological terms; and by ascertaining experimentally what intellectual t
136.5: asks children of different ages can perform, we are, of course, able to make our age standards as definite as we please. Why sho
136.6: uld a device so simple have waited so long for a discoverer? We do not know. It is of a class with many other unaccountable myst
136.7: eries in the development of scientific method. Apparently the idea of an agegrade method, as this is called, did not come to Bin
136.8: et himself until he had experimented with intelligence tests for some fifteen years. At least his first provisional scale, publi
136.9: shed in 1905, was not made up according to the agegrade plan. It consisted merely of 30 tests, arranged roughly in order of diff
136.10: iculty. Although Binet nowhere gives any account of the steps by which this crude and ungraded scale was transformed into the re
136.11: latively complete agegrade scale of 1908, we can infer that the original and ingenious idea of utilizing age norms was suggested
136.12: by the data collected with the 1905 scale. However the discovery was made, it ranks, perhaps, from the practical point of view,
136.13: as the most important in all the history of psychology. 2. _The kind of mental functions brought into play._ In the second plac
136.14: e, the Binet tests differ from most of the earlier attempts in that they are designed to test the higher and more complex mental
136.15: processes, instead of the simpler and more elementary ones. Hence they set problems for the reasoning powers and ingenuity, pro
136.16: voke judgments about abstract matters, etc., instead of attempting to measure sensory discrimination, mere retentiveness, rapidi
136.17: ty of reaction, and the like. Psychologists had generally considered the higher processes too complex to be measured directly, a
136.18: nd accordingly sought to get at them indirectly by correlating supposed intelligence with simpler processes which could readily
136.19: be measured, such as reaction time, rapidity of tapping, discrimination of tones and colors, etc. While they were disputing over
136.20: their contradictory findings in this line of exploration, Binet went directly to the point and succeeded where they had failed.
136.21: It is now generally admitted by psychologists that higher intelligence is little concerned in such elementary processes as thos
136.22: e mentioned above. Many of the animals have keen sensory discrimination. Feebleminded children, unless of very low grade, do not
136.23: differ very markedly from normal children in sensitivity of the skin, visual acuity, simple reaction time, type of imagery, etc
136.24: . But in power of comprehension, abstraction, and ability to direct thought, in the nature of the associative processes, in amou
136.25: nt of information possessed, and in spontaneity of attention, they differ enormously. 3. _Binet would test "general intelligence
136.26: ."_ Finally, Binet's success was largely due to his abandonment of the older "faculty psychology" which, far from being defunct,
136.27: had really given direction to most of the earlier work with mental tests. Where others had attempted to measure memory attentio
136.28: n, sense discrimination, etc., as separate faculties or functions, Binet undertook to ascertain the _general level_ of intellige
136.29: nce. Others had thought the task easier of accomplishment by measuring each division or aspect of intelligence separately, and s
136.30: ummating the results. Binet, too, began in this way, and it was only after years of experimentation by the usual methods that he
136.31: finally broke away from them and undertook, so to speak, to triangulate the height of his tower without first getting the dimen
136.32: sions of the individual stones which made it up. The assumption that it is easier to measure a part, or one aspect, of intellige
136.33: nce than all of it, is fallacious in that the parts are not separate parts and cannot be separated by any refinement of experime
136.34: nt. They are interwoven and intertwined. Each ramifies everywhere and appears in all other functions. The analogy of the stones
136.35: of the tower does not really apply. Memory, for example, cannot be tested separately from attention, or sensediscrimination sepa
136.36: rately from the associative processes. After many vain attempts to disentangle the various intellective functions, Binet decided
136.37: to test their combined functional capacity without any pretense of measuring the exact contribution of each to the total produc
136.38: t. It is hardly too much to say that intelligence tests have been successful just to the extent to which they have been guided b
136.39: y this aim. Memory, attention, imagination, etc., are terms of "structural psychology." Binet's psychology is dynamic. He concei
136.40: ves intelligence as the sum total of those thought processes which consist in mental adaptation. This adaptation is not explicab
136.41: le in terms of the old mental "faculties." No one of these can explain a single thought process, for such process always involve
136.42: s the participation of many functions whose separate rôles are impossible to distinguish accurately. Instead of measuring the in
136.43: tensity of various mental states (psychophysics), it is more enlightening to measure their combined effect on adaptation. Using
136.44: a biological comparison, Binet says the old "faculties" correspond to the separate tissues of an animal or plant, while his own
136.45: "scheme of thought" corresponds to the functioning organ itself. For Binet, psychology is the science of behavior. BINET'S CONCE
136.46: PTION OF GENERAL INTELLIGENCE. In devising tests of intelligence it is, of course, necessary to be guided by some assumption, or
136.47: assumptions, regarding the nature of intelligence. To adopt any other course is to depend for success upon happy chance. Howeve
136.48: r, it is impossible to arrive at a final definition of intelligence on the basis of _apriori_ considerations alone. To demand, a
136.49: s critics of the Binet method have sometimes done, that one who would measure intelligence should first present a complete defin
136.50: ition of it, is quite unreasonable. As Stern points out, electrical currents were measured long before their nature was well und
136.51: erstood. Similar illustrations could be drawn from the processes involved in chemistry physiology, and other sciences. In the ca
136.52: se of intelligence it may be truthfully said that no adequate definition can possibly be framed which is not based primarily on
136.53: the symptoms empirically brought to light by the test method. The best that can be done in advance of such data is to make tenta
136.54: tive assumptions as to the probable nature of intelligence, and then to subject these assumptions to tests which will show their
136.55: correctness or incorrectness. New hypotheses can then be framed for further trial, and thus gradually we shall be led to a conc
136.56: eption of intelligence which will be meaningful and in harmony with all the ascertainable facts. Such was the method of Binet. O
136.57: nly those unacquainted with Binet's more than fifteen years of labor preceding the publication of his intelligence scale would t
136.58: hink of accusing him of making no effort to analyze the mental processes which his tests bring into play. It is true that many o
136.59: f Binet's earlier assumptions proved untenable, and in this event he was always ready, with exceptional candor and intellectual
136.60: plasticity, to acknowledge his error and to plan a new line of attack. Binet's conception of intelligence emphasizes three chara
136.61: cteristics of the thought process: (1) Its tendency to take and maintain a definite direction; (2) the capacity to make adaptati
136.62: ons for the purpose of attaining a desired end; and (3) the power of autocriticism.[11] [11] See Binet and Simon: "L'intelligenc
136.63: e des imbeciles," in _L'Année Psychologique_ (1909), pp. 1147. The last division of this article is devoted to a discussion of t
136.64: he essential nature of the higher thought processes, and is a wonderful example of that keen psychological analysis in which Bin

137.1: et was so gifted. How these three aspects of intelligence enter into the performances with various tests of the scale is set for
137.2: th from time to time in our directions for giving and interpreting the individual tests.[12] An illustration which may be given
137.3: here is that of the "patience test," or uniting the disarranged parts of a divided rectangle. As described by Binet, this operat
137.4: ion has the following elements: "(1) to keep in mind the end to be attained, that is to say, the figure to be formed; (2) to try
137.5: different combinations under the influence of this directing idea, which guides the efforts of the subject even though he may n
137.6: ot be conscious of the fact; and (3) to judge the combination which has been made, to compare it with the model, and to decide w
137.7: hether it is the correct one." [12] See especially pages 162 and 238. Much the same processes are called for in many other of th
137.8: e Binet tests, particularly those of arranging weights, rearranging dissected sentences, drawing a diamond or square from copy,
137.9: finding a sentence containing three given words, counting backwards, etc. However, an examination of the scale will show that th
137.10: e choice of tests was not guided entirely by any single formula as to the nature of intelligence. Binet's approach was a manysid
137.11: ed one. The scale includes tests of time orientation, of three or four kinds of memory, of apperception, of language comprehensi
137.12: on, of knowledge about common objects, of free association, of number mastery, of constructive imagination, and of ability to co
137.13: mpare concepts, to see contradictions, to combine fragments into a unitary whole, to comprehend abstract terms, and to meet nove
137.14: l situations. OTHER CONCEPTIONS OF INTELLIGENCE. It is interesting to compare Binet's conception of intelligence with the defini
137.15: tions which have been offered by other psychologists. According to Ebbinghaus, for example, the essence of intelligence lies in
137.16: comprehending together in a unitary, meaningful whole, impressions and associations which are more or less independent, heteroge
137.17: neous, or even partly contradictory. "Intellectual ability consists in the elaboration of a whole into its worth and meaning by
137.18: means of manysided combination, correction, and completion of numerous kindred associations.... It is a _combination activity_."
137.19: Meumann offers a twofold definition. From the psychological point of view, intelligence is the power of independent and creativ
137.20: e elaboration of new products out of the material given by memory and the senses. From the practical point of view, it involves
137.21: the ability to avoid errors, to surmount difficulties, and to adjust to environment. Stern defines intelligence as "the general
137.22: capacity of an individual consciously to adjust his thinking to new requirements: it is general adaptability to new problems and
137.23: conditions of life." Spearman, Hart, and others of the English school define intelligence as a "common central factor" which pa
137.24: rticipates in all sorts of special mental activities. This factor is explained in terms of a psychophysiological hypothesis of "
137.25: cortex energy," "cerebral plasticity," etc. The above definitions are only to a slight extent contradictory or inharmonious. The
137.26: y differ mainly in point of view or in the location of the emphasis. Each expresses a part of the truth, and none all of it. It
137.27: will be evident that the conception of Binet is broad enough to include the most important elements in each of the other definit
137.28: ions quoted. GUIDING PRINCIPLES IN CHOICE AND ARRANGEMENT OF TESTS. In choosing his tests Binet was guided by the conception of
137.29: intelligence which we have set forth above. Tests were devised which would presumably bring into play the various mental process
137.30: es thought to be concerned in intelligence, and then these tests were tried out on normal children of different ages. If the per
137.31: centage of passes for a given test increased but little or not at all in going from younger to older children this test was disc
137.32: arded. On the other hand, if the proportion of passes increased rapidly with age, and if children of a given age, who on other g
137.33: rounds were known to be bright, passed more frequently than children of the same age who were known to be dull, then the test wa
137.34: s judged a satisfactory test of intelligence. As we have shown elsewhere,[13] practically all of Binet's tests fulfill these req
137.35: uirements reasonably well, a fact which bears eloquent testimony to the keen psychological insight of their author. [13] See p.
137.36: 55. In arranging the tests into a system Binet's guiding principle was to find an arrangement of the tests which would cause an
137.37: average child of any given age to test "at age"; that is, the average 5yearold must show a mental age of 5 years, the average 8y
137.38: earold a mental age of 8 years, etc. In order to secure this result Binet found that his data seemed to require the location of
137.39: an individual test in that year where it was passed by about two thirds to three fourths of unselected children. It was in the a
137.40: ssembling of the tests that the most serious faults of the scale had their origin. Further investigation has shown that a great
137.41: many of the tests were misplaced as much as one year, and several of them two years. On the whole, the scale as Binet left it wa
137.42: s decidedly too easy in the lower ranges, and too difficult in the upper. As a result, the average child of 5 years was caused t
137.43: o test at not far from 6 years, the average child of 12 years not far from 11. In the Stanford revision an effort has been made
137.44: to correct this fault, along with certain other generally recognized imperfections. SOME AVOWED LIMITATIONS OF THE BINET TESTS.
137.45: The Binet tests have often been criticized for their unfitness to perform certain services which in reality they were never mean
137.46: t to render. This is unfair. We cannot make a just evaluation of the scale without bearing in mind its avowed limitations. For e
137.47: xample, the scale does not pretend to measure the entire mentality of the subject, but only _general intelligence_. There is no
137.48: pretense of testing the emotions or the will beyond the extent to which these naturally display themselves in the tests of intel
137.49: ligence. The scale was not designed as a tool for the analysis of those emotional or volitional aberrations which are concerned
137.50: in such mental disorders as hysteria, insanity, etc. These conditions do not present a progressive reduction of intelligence to
137.51: the infantile level, and in most of them other factors besides intelligence play an important rôle. Moreover, even in the normal
137.52: individual the fruitfulness of intelligence, the direction in which it shall be applied, and its methods of work are to a certa
137.53: in extent determined by the extraneous factors of emotion and volition. It should, nevertheless, be pointed out that defects of
137.54: intelligence, in a large majority of cases, also involve disturbances of the emotional and volitional functions. We do not expec
137.55: t to find perfectly normal emotions or will power of average strength coupled with marked intellectual deficiency, and as a matt
137.56: er of fact such a combination is rare indeed. In the course of an examination with the Binet tests, the experienced clinical psy
137.57: chologist is able to gain considerable insight into the subject's emotional and volitional equipment, even though the method was
137.58: designed primarily for another purpose. A second misunderstanding can be avoided by remembering that the Binet scale does not p
137.59: retend to bring to light the idiosyncrasies of special talent, but only to measure the general level of intelligence. It cannot
137.60: be used for the discovery of exceptional ability in drawing, painting, music, mathematics, oratory, salesmanship, etc., because
137.61: no effort is made to explore the processes underlying these abilities. It can, therefore, never serve as a _detailed chart_ for
137.62: the vocational guidance of children, telling us which will succeed in business, which in art, which in medicine, etc. It is not
137.63: a new kind of phrenology. At the same time, as we have already pointed out, _it is capable of bounding roughly the vocational te
137.64: rritory in which an individual's intelligence will probably permit success, nothing else preventing_.[14] [14] See p. 17. In the

138.1: third place, it must not be supposed that the scale can be used as a complete pedagogical guide. Although intelligence tests fu
138.2: rnish data of the greatest significance for pedagogical procedure, they do not suggest the appropriate educational methods in de
138.3: tail. These will have to be worked out in a practical way for the various grades of intelligence, and at great cost of labor and
138.4: patience. Finally, in arriving at an estimate of a subject's grade of intelligence and his susceptibility to training, it would
138.5: be a mistake to ignore the data obtainable from other sources. No competent psychologist, however ardent a supporter of the Bin
138.6: et method he might be, would recommend such a policy. Those who accept the method as allsufficient are as much in error as those
138.7: who consider it as no more important than any one of a dozen other approaches. Standardized tests have already become and will
138.8: remain by far the most reliable single method for grading intelligence, but the results they furnish will always need to be inte
138.9: rpreted in the light of supplementary information regarding the subject's personal history, including medical record, accidents,
138.10: play habits, industrial efficiency, social and moral traits, school success, home environment, etc. Without question, however,
138.11: the improved Binet tests will contribute more than all other data combined to the end of enabling us to forecast a child's possi
138.12: bilities of future improvement, and this is the information which will aid most in the proper direction of his education. CHAPTE

138.52: ce quotient,[16] a correct scale must give a median intelligence quotient of unity, or 100 per cent, for unselected children of

152.4: to the influence of school and home environment as seriously to invalidate the scale as a whole. Some of the tests most often n
152.5: amed in this connection are the following: Giving age and sex; naming common objects, colors, and coins; giving the value of sta
152.6: mps; giving date; naming the months of the year and the days of the week; distinguishing forenoon and afternoon; counting; makin
152.7: g change; reading for memories; naming sixty words; giving definitions; finding rhymes; and constructing a sentence containing t
152.8: hree given words. It has in fact been found wherever comparisons have been made that children of superior social status yield a

152.10: net himself may be referred to in this connection. In the case of the Stanford investigation, also, it was found that when the u
152.11: nselected school children were grouped in three classes according to social status (superior, average, and inferior), the averag
152.12: e I Q for the superior social group was 107, and that of the inferior social group 93. This is equivalent to a difference of one
152.13: year in mental age with 7yearolds, and to a difference of two years with 14yearolds. However, the common opinion that the child
152.14: from a cultured home does better in tests solely by reason of his superior home advantages is an entirely gratuitous assumption
152.15: . Practically all of the investigations which have been made of the influence of nature and nurture on mental performance agree
152.16: in attributing far more to original endowment than to environments. Common observation would itself suggest that the social clas
152.17: s to which the family belongs depends less on chance than on the parents' native qualities of intellect and character. The resul
152.18: ts of five separate and distinct lines of inquiry based on the Stanford data agree in supporting the conclusion that the childre
152.19: n of successful and cultured parents test higher than children from wretched and ignorant homes for the simple reason that their

152.21: Extension of the BinetSimon Measuring Scale of Intelligence_. (Warwick and York, 1916) It would, of course, be going too far to
152.22: deny all possibility of environmental conditions affecting the result of an intelligence test. Certainly no one would expect tha

152.26: school in a civilized community, affects to any great extent the validity of the scale. A crucial experiment would be to take a
152.27: large number of very young children of the lower classes and, after placing them in the most favorable environment obtainable,
152.28: to compare their later mental development with that of children born into the best homes. No extensive study of this kind has be
152.29: en made, but the writer has tested twenty orphanage children who, for the most part, had come from very inferior homes. They had
152.30: been in a wellconducted orphanage for from two to several years, and had enjoyed during that time the advantages of an excellen
152.31: t village school. Nevertheless, all but three tested below average, ranging from 75 to 90 I Q. The impotence of school instructi
152.32: on to neutralize individual differences in native endowment will be evident to any one who follows the school career of backward
152.33: children. The children who are seriously retarded in school are not normal, and cannot be made normal by any refinement of educ
152.34: ational method. As a rule, the longer the inferior child attends school, the more evident his inferiority becomes. It would hard
152.35: ly be reasonable, therefore, to expect that a little incidental instruction in the home would weigh very heavily against these s
152.36: ame native differences in endowment. Cases like the following show conclusively that it does not: X is the son of unusually inte
152.37: lligent and welleducated parents. The home is everything one would expect of people of scholarly pursuits and cultivated tastes.
152.38: But X has always been irresponsible, troublesome, childish, and queer. He learned to walk at 2 years, to talk at 3, and has alw
152.39: ays been delicate and nervous. When brought for examination he was 8 years old. He had twice attempted school work, but could ac
152.40: complish nothing and was withdrawn. His playlife was not normal, and other children, younger than himself, abused and tormented
152.41: him. The Binet tests gave an I Q of approximately 75; that is, the retardation amounted to about two years. The child was examin
152.42: ed again three years later. At that time, after attending school two years, he had recently completed the first grade. This time
152.43: the I Q was 73. Strange to say, the mother is encouraged and hopeful because she sees that her boy is learning to read. She doe
152.44: s not seem to realize that at his age he ought to be within three years of entering high school. The fortyminute test had told m
152.45: ore about the mental ability of this boy than the intelligent mother had been able to learn in eleven years of daily and hourly
152.46: observation. For X is feebleminded; he will never complete the grammar school; he will never be an efficient worker or a respons
152.47: ible citizen. Let us change the picture. Z is a brighteyed, darkskinned girl of 9 years. She is darkskinned because her father i
152.48: s a mixture of Indian and Spanish. The mother is of Irish descent. With her strangely mated parents and two brothers she lives i
152.49: n a dirty, cramped, and poorly furnished house in the country. The parents are illiterate, and the brothers are retarded and dul
152.50: l, though not feebleminded. It is Z's turn to be tested. I inquire the name. It is familiar, for I have already tested the two s
152.51: tupid brothers. I also know her ignorant parents and the miserable cabin in which she lives. The examination begins with the 8ye
152.52: ar tests. The responses are quick and accurate. We proceed to the 9year group. There is no failure, and there is but one minor e
152.53: rror. Successes and failures alternate for a while until the latter prevail. Z has tested at 11 years. In spite of her wretched
152.54: home, she is mentally advanced nearly 25 per cent. By the vocabulary test she is credited with a knowledge of nearly 6000 words,
152.55: or nearly four times as many as X, the boy of cultured home and scholarly parents, had learned by the age of 8 years. Five year
152.56: s have passed. When given the test, Z was in the fourth grade and, as we have already stated, 9 years of age. As a result of the
152.57: test she was transferred to the fifth grade. Later she skipped again and at the age of 14 is a successful student in the second
152.58: year of high school. To assay her intelligence and determine its quality was a task of fortyfive minutes. The above cases, each
152.59: of which could be paralleled by many others which we have found, will serve to illustrate the fact that exceptionally superior
152.60: endowment is discoverable by the tests, however unfavorable the home from which it comes, and that inferior endowment cannot be
152.61: normalized by all the advantages of the most cultured home. Quoting again from Stern, "The tests actually reach and discover the
152.62: general developmental conditions of intelligence, and not mere fragments of knowledge and attainments acquired by chance." PART

152.64: ND EFFORT. The child's intelligence is to be judged by his success in the performance of certain tasks. These tasks may appear t

153.1: o the examiner to be very easy, indeed; but we must bear in mind that they are often anything but easy for the child. Real effor
153.2: t and attention are necessary for his success, and occasionally even his best efforts fall short of the desired result. If the t
153.3: ests are to display the child's real intellectual ability it will be necessary, therefore, to avoid as nearly as possible every
153.4: disturbing factor which would divide his attention or in any other way injure the quality of his responses. To insure this it wi
153.5: ll be necessary to consider somewhat in detail a number of factors which influence effort, such as degree of quiet, the nature o
153.6: f surroundings, presence or absence of others, means of gaining the child's confidence, the avoidance of embarrassment, fatigue,
153.7: etc. One should not expect, however, to secure an absolutely equal degree of attention from all subjects. The power to give sus
153.8: tained attention to a difficult task is characteristically weak in dull and feebleminded children. What we should labor to secur
153.9: e is the maximum attention of which the child is capable, and if this is unsatisfactory without external cause, we are to regard
153.10: the fact as symptomatic of inferior mental ability, not as an extenuating factor or an excuse for lack of success in the tests.
153.11: Attention, of course, cannot be normal if any acute physical or mental disturbance is present. Toothache, headache, earache, na
153.12: usea, fever, cold, etc., all render the test inadvisable. The same is true of mental anxiety or fear, as in the case of the chil
153.13: d who has just been arrested and brought before the court. QUIET AND SECLUSION. The tests should be conducted in a quiet room, l
153.14: ocated where the noises of the street and other outside distractions cannot enter. A reasonably small room is better than a very
153.15: large one, because it is more homelike. The furnishings of the room should be simple. A table and two chairs are sufficient. If
153.16: the room contains a number of unfamiliar objects, such as psychological apparatus, pictures on the walls, etc., the attention o
153.17: f the child is likely to be drawn away from the tasks which he is given to do. The halls and corridors which it is sometimes nec
153.18: essary to use in testing school children are usually noisy, cold, or otherwise objectionable. PRESENCE OF OTHERS. A still more d
153.19: isturbing influence is the presence of other persons. Generally speaking, if accurate results are to be secured it is not permis
153.20: sible to have any auditor, besides possibly an assistant to record the responses. Even the assistant, however quiet and unobtrus
153.21: ive, is sometimes a disturbing element. Though something of a convenience, the assistant is by no means necessary, after the exa
153.22: miner has thoroughly mastered the procedure of the tests and has acquired some skill in the use of abbreviations in recording th
153.23: e answers. If an assistant or any other person is present, he should be seated somewhat behind the child, not too close, and sho
153.24: uld take no notice of the child either when he enters the room or at any time during the examination. At all events, the presenc
153.25: e of parent, teacher, school principal, or governess is to be avoided. Contrary to what one might expect, these distract the chi
153.26: ld much more than a strange personality would do. Their critical attitude toward the child's performance is very likely to cause
153.27: embarrassment. If the child is alone with the examiner, he is more at ease from the mere fact that he does not feel that there
153.28: is a reputation to sustain. The praise so lavishly bestowed upon him by the friendly and sympathetic examiner lends to the same
153.29: effect. As Binet emphasizes, if the presence of others cannot be avoided, it is at least necessary to require of them absolute s
153.30: ilence. Parents, and sometimes teachers, have an almost irrepressible tendency to interrupt the examination with excuses for the
153.31: child's failures and with disturbing explanations which are likely to aid the child in comprehending the required task. Without
153.32: the least intention of doing so, they sometimes practically tell the child how to respond. Parents, especially, cannot refrain
153.33: from scolding the child or showing impatience when his answers do not come up to expectation. This, of course, endangers the chi
153.34: ld's success still further. The psychologist is not surprised at such conduct. It would be foolish to expect average parents, ev
153.35: en apart from their bias in the particular case at hand, to adopt the scientific attitude of the trained examiner. Since we cann
153.36: ot in a few moments at our disposal make them over into psychologists, our only recourse is to deal with them by exclusion. This
153.37: is not to say that it is impossible to test a child satisfactorily in the presence of others. If the examiner is experienced, a
153.38: nd if the child is not timid, it is sometimes possible to make a successful test in the presence of quite a number of auditors,
153.39: provided they remain silent, refrain from staring, and otherwise conduct themselves with discretion. But not even the veteran ex
153.40: aminer can always be sure of the outcome in demonstration testing. GETTING INTO "RAPPORT." The examiner's first task is to win t
153.41: he confidence of the child and overcome his timidity. Unless _rapport_ has first been established, the results of the first test
153.42: s given are likely to be misleading. The time and effort necessary for accomplishing this are variable factors, depending upon t
153.43: he personality of both the examiner and the subject. In a majority of cases from three to five minutes should be sufficient, but
153.44: in a few cases somewhat more time is necessary. The writer has found that when a strange child is brought to the clinic for exa
153.45: mination, it is advantageous to go out of doors with him for a little walk around the university buildings. It is usually possib
153.46: le to return from such a stroll in a few minutes, with the child chattering away as though to an old friend. Another approach is
153.47: to begin by showing the child some interesting object, such as a toy, or a formboard, or pictures not used in the test. The onl
153.48: y danger in this method is that the child is likely to find the object so interesting that he may not be willing to abandon it f
153.49: or the tests, or that his mind will keep reverting to it during the examination. Still another method is to give the child his s
153.50: eat as soon as he is ushered into the room, and, after a word of greeting, which must be spoken in a kindly tone but without gus
153.51: hiness, to open up a conversation about matters likely to be of interest. The weather, place of residence, pets, sports, games,
153.52: toys, travels, current events, etc., are suitable topics if rightly employed. When the child has begun to express himself withou
153.53: t timidity and it is clear that his confidence has been gained, one may proceed, as though in continuance of the conversation, t
153.54: o inquire the name, age, and school grade. The examiner notes these down in the appropriate blanks, rather unconcernedly, at the
153.55: same time complimenting the child (unless it is clearly a case of serious retardation) on the fine progress he has made with hi
153.56: s studies. KEEPING THE CHILD ENCOURAGED. Nothing contributes more to a satisfactory _rapport_ than praise of the child's efforts
153.57: . Under no circumstances should the examiner permit himself to show displeasure at a response, however absurd it may be. In gene
153.58: ral, the poorer the response, the better satisfied one should appear to be with it. An error is always to be passed by without c
153.59: omment, unless it is painfully evident to the child himself, in which case the examiner will do well to make some excuse for it;
153.60: e.g., "You are not quite old enough to answer questions like that one; but, never mind, you are doing beautifully," etc. Exclam
153.61: ations like "fine!" "splendid!" etc., should be used lavishly. Almost any innocent deception is permissible which keeps the chil
153.62: d interested, confident, and at his best level of effort. The examination should begin with tests that are fairly easy, in order
153.63: to give the child a little experience with success before the more difficult tests are reached. THE IMPORTANCE OF TACT. It goes
153.64: without saying that children's personalities are not so uniform and simple that we can adhere always to a single stereotyped pr

154.1: ocedure in working our way into their good graces. Suggestions like the above have their value, but, like rules of etiquette, th
154.2: ey must be supported by the tact which comes of intuition and cannot be taught. The address which flatters and pleases one child
154.3: may excite disgust in another. The examiner must scent the situation and adapt his method to it. One child is timid and embarra
154.4: ssed; another may think his mental powers are under suspicion and so react with sullen obstinacy; a third may be in an angry moo
154.5: d as a result of a recent playground quarrel. Situations like these are, of course, exceptional, but in any case it is necessary
154.6: to create in the child a certain mood, or indefinable attitude of mind, before the test begins. PERSONALITY OF THE EXAMINER. Do
154.7: ubtless there are persons so lacking in personal adaptability that success in this kind of work would be for them impossible. Th
154.8: e wooden, mechanical, matteroffact and unresponsive personality is as much out of place in the psychological clinic as the tradi
154.9: tional bull in the china shop. It would make an interesting study for some one to investigate, by exact methods, the influence o
154.10: n test results of the personality of different examiners who have been equally trained in the methods to be employed and who are
154.11: equally conscientious in applying them according to rules. On the whole, differences of this kind are probably not very great a
154.12: mong experienced and reasonably competent examiners. Adaptability grows with experience and with increase of selfconfidence. Aft
154.13: er a few score tests there should be no serious failure from inability to get into _rapport_ with the child. Even in those rare
154.14: cases where the child breaks down and cries from timidity, or perhaps refuses to answer out of embarrassment, the difficulty can
154.15: be overcome by sufficient tact so that the examination may proceed as though nothing had happened. If the examiner has the prop
154.16: er psychological and personal equipment, the testing of twenty or thirty children forms a fairly satisfactory apprenticeship. Wi
154.17: thout psychological training, no amount of experience will guarantee absolute accuracy of the results. THE AVOIDANCE OF FATIGUE.
154.18: Against the validity of intelligence tests it is often argued that the result of an examination depends a great deal on the tim
154.19: e of day when it is made, whether in the morning hours when the mind is at its best, or in the afternoon when it is supposedly f
154.20: atigued. Although no very extensive investigation has been made of this influence, there is no evidence that the ordinary fatigu
154.21: e incident to school work injures the child's performance appreciably. Our tests of 1000 children showed no inferiority of resul
154.22: ts secured from 1 to 4 P.M., as compared with tests made from 9 to 12 A.M. An explanation for this is not hard to find. Although
154.23: school work causes fatigue, in the sense that a part of the child's available supply of mental energy is used up, there is alwa
154.24: ys a reserve of energy sufficient to carry the child through a thirtyto fiftyminute test. The fact that the required tasks are n
154.25: ovel and interesting to a high degree insures that the reserve energy will really be brought into play. This principle, of cours
154.26: e, has its natural limits. The examiner would avoid testing a child who was exhausted either from work or play, or a child who w
154.27: as noticeably sleepy. DURATION OF THE EXAMINATION. About the only danger of fatigue lies in making the examination too long. You
154.28: ng children show symptoms of weariness much more quickly than older children, and it is therefore fortunate that not so much tim

154.32: child, in addition to that actually consumed in the tests. But the examiner need not expect to hold fast to any schedule. Some s

154.34: wly, but exceptions to this rule are not uncommon. One 8yearold boy examined by the writer answered so hesitatingly that it requ

154.41: e purse, and the pictures, colors, stamps, and designs for drawing should be mounted on stiff cardboard which may be punched and

154.45: rd booklet which has been specially devised for testing with the Stanford revision. It contains all the necessary printed materi

154.60: ng normal children, little error will result if we go back no farther than the year which yielded only one failure, and if we st

154.62: e uneven mentally than normal children, and therefore scatter their successes and failures over a wider range. With such subject

155.1: he child's conversation and conduct and to dispense with most of this preliminary exploration. ORDER OF GIVING THE TESTS. The ch
155.2: ild's efforts in the tests are sometimes markedly influenced by the order in which they are given. If language tests or memory t
155.3: ests are given first, the child is likely to be embarrassed. More suitable to begin with are those which test knowledge or judgm

155.6: rences or similarities, making sentences, repeating sentences, and drawing are especially unsuitable because they tend to provok
155.7: e selfconsciousness. The tests as arranged in this revision are in the order which it is usually best to follow, but one should
155.8: not hesitate to depart from the order given when it seems best in a given case to do so. It is necessary to be constantly alert
155.9: so that when the child shows a tendency to balk at a given type of test, such as those of memory, language, numbers, drawing, "c
155.10: omprehension," etc., the work can be shifted to more agreeable tasks. When the child is at his ease again, it is usually possibl
155.11: e to return to the troublesome tests with better success. In the case of 8yearold D. C., who is a speech defective but otherwise
155.12: above normal, it was quite impossible at the first sitting to give such tests as sentencemaking, naming sixty words, reading, r
155.13: epeating sentences, giving definitions, etc.; at each test of this type the child's voice broke and he was ready to cry, due, no
155.14: doubt, to sensitiveness regarding his speech defect. Others do everything willingly except the drawing and copying. The younger
155.15: children sometimes refuse to repeat the sentences or digits. In all such cases it is best to pass on to something else. After a
155.16: few minutes the rejected task may be done willingly. COAXING TO BE AVOIDED. Although we should always encourage the child to be
155.17: lieve that he can answer correctly, if he will only try, we must avoid the common practice of dragging out responses by too much
155.18: urging and coaxing. The sympathies of the examiner tend to lead him into the habit of repeating and explaining the question if
155.19: the child does not answer promptly. This is nearly always a mistake, for the question is one which should be understood. Besides
155.20: , explanations and coaxing are too often equivalent to answering the question for the child. It is almost impossible to impress
155.21: this danger sufficiently upon the untrained examiner. One who is not familiar with the psychology of suggestion may put the answ
155.22: er in the child's mouth without suspecting what he is doing. ADHERING TO FORMULA. It cannot be too strongly emphasized that unle
155.23: ss we follow a standardized procedure the tests lose their significance. The danger is chiefly that of unintentionally and uncon
155.24: sciously introducing variations which will affect the meaning of the test. One who has not had a thorough training in the method
155.25: s of mental testing cannot appreciate how numerous are the opportunities for the unconscious transformation of a test. Many of t
155.26: hese are pointed out in the description of the individual tests, but it would be folly to undertake to warn the experimenter aga
155.27: inst every possible error of this kind. Sometimes the omission or the addition of a single phrase in giving the test will alter
155.28: materially the significance of the response. Only the trained psychologist can vary the formula without risk of invalidating the
155.29: result, and even he must be on his guard. All sorts of misunderstandings regarding the correct placing of tests and regarding t
155.30: heir accuracy or inaccuracy have come about through the failure of different investigators to follow the same procedure. One who
155.31: would use the tests for any serious purpose, therefore, must study the procedure for each and every test until he knows it thor
155.32: oughly. After that a considerable amount of practice is necessary before one learns to avoid slips. During the early stages of p
155.33: ractice it is necessary to refer to the printed instructions frequently in order to check up errors before they have become habi
155.34: tual. The instructions hitherto available are at fault in not defining the procedure with sufficient definiteness, and it is the
155.35: purpose of this volume to make good this deficiency as far as possible. It is too much, however, to suppose that the instructio
155.36: ns can be made "foolproof." With whatever definiteness they may be set forth, situations are sure to arise which the examiner ca
155.37: nnot be formally prepared for. There is no limit to the multitude of misunderstandings possible. After testing hundreds of child
155.38: ren one still finds new examples of misapprehension. In a few such cases the instruction may be repeated, if there is reason to
155.39: think the child's hearing was at fault or if some extraordinary distraction has occurred. But unless otherwise stated in the dir
155.40: ections, the repetition of a question is ordinarily to be avoided. Supplementary explanations are hardly ever permissible. In sh
155.41: ort, numberless situations may arise in the use of a test which may injure the validity of the response, events which cannot alw
155.42: ays be dealt with by preconceived rule. Accordingly, although we must urge unceasingly the importance of following the standard
155.43: procedure, it is not to be supposed that formulas are an adequate substitute either for scientific judgment or for common sense.
155.44: SCORING. The exact method of scoring the individual tests is set forth in the following chapters. Reference to the record bookl
155.45: et for use in testing will show that the records are to be kept in detail. Each subdivision of a test should be scored separatel
155.46: y, in order that the clinical picture may be as complete as possible. This helps in the final evaluation of the results. It make
155.47: s much difference, for example, whether success in repeating six digits is earned by repeating all three correctly or only one;
155.48: or whether the child's lack of success with the absurdities is due to failure on two, three, four, or all of them. Time should b
155.49: e recorded whenever called for in the record blanks. RECORDING RESPONSES. Plus and minus signs alone are not usually sufficient.

157.22: about a child's intelligence status. The significance of a given number of years of retardation or acceleration depends upon the
157.23: age of the child. A 3yearold child who is retarded one year is ordinarily feebleminded; a 10yearold retarded one year is only a
157.24: little below normal. The child who at 3 years of age is retarded one year will probably be retarded two years at the age of 6,
157.25: three years at the age of 9, and four years at the age of 12. What we want to know, therefore, is the ratio existing between men
157.26: tal age and real age. This is the intelligence quotient, or I Q. To find it we simply divide mental age (expressed in years and
157.27: months) by real age (also expressed in years and months). The process is easier if we express each age in terms of months alone
157.28: before dividing. The division can, of course, be performed almost instantaneously and with much less danger of error by the use
157.29: of a slide rule or a division table. One who has to calculate many intelligence quotients should by all means use some kind of m
157.30: echanical help. HOW TO FIND THE I Q OF ADULT SUBJECTS. Native intelligence, in so far as it can be measured by tests now availab
157.31: le, appears to improve but little after the age of 15 or 16 years. It follows that in calculating the I Q of an adult subject, i
157.32: t will be necessary to disregard the years he has lived beyond the point where intelligence attains its final development. Altho
157.33: ugh the location of this point is not exactly known, it will be sufficiently accurate for our purpose to assume its location at
157.34: 16 years. Accordingly, any person over 16 years of age, however old, is for purposes of calculating I Q considered to be just 16
157.35: years old. If a youth of 18 and a man of 60 years both have a mental age of 12 years, the I Q in each case is 12 ÷ 16, or .75.
