163.3: _pencil_, and _table_. Say: "_You have seen a chair. You know what a chair is. Tell me, what is a chair?_" And so on with the ot
163.4: her words, always in the order in which they are named above. Occasionally there is difficulty in getting a response, which is s
163.5: ometimes due merely to the child's unwillingness to express his thoughts in sentences. The earlier tests require only words and
163.6: phrases. In other cases silence is due to the rather indefinite form of the question. The child could answer, but is not quite s
163.7: ure what is expected of him. Whatever the cause, a little tactful urging is nearly always sufficient to bring a response. In thi
163.8: s test we have not found the difficulty of overcoming silence nearly as great as others have stated it to be. In consecutive tes
163.9: ts of 150 5 and 6yearold children we encountered unbreakable silence with 8 words out of the total 900 (150 × 6). This is less t
163.10: han 1 per cent. But tactful encouragement is sometimes necessary, and it is best to take the precaution of not giving the test u
163.11: ntil _rapport_ has been well established. The urging should take the following form: "_I'm sure you know what a ... is. You have
163.12: seen a .... Now, tell me, what is a ... ?_" That is, we merely repeat the question with a word of encouragement and in a coaxin
163.13: g tone of voice. It would not at all do to introduce other questions, like, "_What does a ... look like?_" or, "_What is a ... f
163.14: or?_" "_What do people do with a ... ?_" Sometimes, instead of attempting a definition (of _doll_, for example), the child begin
163.15: s to talk in a more or less irrelevant way, as "I have a great big doll. Auntie gave it to me for Christmas," etc. In such cases
163.16: we repeat the question and say, "_Yes, but tell me; what is a doll?_" This is usually sufficient to bring the little chatterbox
163.17: back to the task. Unless it is absolutely necessary to give the child lavish encouragement, it is best to withhold approval or
163.18: disapproval until the test has been finished. If the first response is a poor one and we pronounce it "fine" or "very good," we
163.19: tempt the child to persist in his lowgrade type of definition. By withholding comment until the last word has been defined, we g
163.20: ive greater play to spontaneity and initiative. SCORING. As a rule, children of 5 and 6 years define an object in terms of use,
163.21: stating what it does, what it is for, what people do with it, etc. Definitions by description, by telling what substance it is m
163.22: ade of, and by giving the class to which it belongs are grouped together as "definitions superior to use." It is not before 8 ye
163.23: ars that two thirds of the children spontaneously give a large proportion of definitions in terms superior to use. The test is p
163.24: assed in year V if _four words out of the six_ are defined in terms of use (or better than use). The following are examples of s
163.25: atisfactory responses: _Chair_: "To sit on." "You sit on it." "It is made of wood and has legs and back," etc. _Horse_: "To driv
163.26: e." "To ride." "What people drive." "To pull the wagon." "It is big and has four legs," etc. _Fork_: "To eat with." "To stick me
163.27: at with." "It is hard and has three sharp things," etc. _Doll_: "To play with." "What you dress and put to bed." "To rock," etc.
163.28: _Pencil_: "To write with." "To draw." "They write with it." "It is sharp and makes a black mark." _Table_: "To eat on." "What y
163.29: ou put the dinner on." "Where you write." "It is made of wood and has legs." Examples of failure are such responses as the follo
163.30: wing: "A chair is a chair"; "There is a chair"; or simply, "There" (pointing to a chair). We record such responses without press
163.31: ing for a further definition. About the only other type of failure is silence. REMARKS. It is not the purpose of this test to fi
163.32: nd out whether the child knows the meaning of the words he is asked to define. Words have purposely been chosen which are perfec
163.33: tly familiar to all normal children of 5 years. But with young children there is a difference between knowing a word and giving
163.34: a definition of it. Besides, we desire to find out how the child apperceives the word, or rather the object for which it stands;
163.35: whether the thing is thought of in terms of use, appearance (shape, size, color, etc.), material composing it, or class relatio
163.36: nships. This test, because it throws such interesting light on the maturity of the child's apperceptive processes, is one of the
163.37: most valuable of all. It is possible to differentiate at least a halfdozen degrees of excellence in definitions, according to t
163.38: he intellectual maturity of the subject. A volume, indeed, could be written on the development of word definitions and the growt
163.39: h of meanings; but we will postpone further discussion until VIII, 5. Our concern at present is to know that children of 5 years
163.40: should at least be able to define four of these six words in terms of use. Binet placed the test in year VI, but our own figure
163.41: s and those of nearly all the other investigations indicate that it is better located in year V. V, 5. THE GAME OF PATIENCE MATE
163.42: RIAL. Prepare two rectangular cards, each 2 × 3 inches, and divide one of them into two triangles by cutting it along one of its
163.43: diagonals. PROCEDURE. Place the uncut card on the table with one of its longer sides to the child. By the side of this card, a
163.44: little nearer the child and a few inches apart, lay the two halves of the divided rectangle with their hypothenuses turned from
163.45: each other as follows: [Illustration] Then say to the child: "_I want you to take these two pieces_ (touching the two triangles)
163.46: _and put them together so they will look exactly like this_" (pointing to the uncut card). If the child hesitates, we repeat th
163.47: e instructions with a little urging. Say nothing about hurrying, as this is likely to cause confusion. Give three trials, of one
163.48: minute each. If only one trial is given, success is too often a result of chance moves; but luck is not likely to bring two suc
163.49: cesses in three trials. If the first trial is a failure, move the cut halves back to their original position and say: "_No; put
163.50: them together so they will look like this_" (pointing to the uncut card). Make no other comment of approval or disapproval. Disr
163.51: egard in silence the inquiring looks of the child who tries to read his success or failure in your face. If one of the pieces is
163.52: turned over, the task becomes impossible, and it is then necessary to turn the piece back to its original position and begin ov
163.53: er, not counting this trial. Have the under side of the pieces marked so as to avoid the risk of presenting one of them to the c
163.54: hild wrong side up. SCORING. There must be _two successes in three trials_. About the only difficulty in scoring is that of deci
163.55: ding what constitutes a trial. We count it a trial when the child brings the pieces together and (after few or many changes) lea
163.56: ves them in some position. Whether he succeeds after many moves, or leaves the pieces with approval in some absurd position, or
163.57: gives up and says he cannot do it, his effort counts as one trial. A single trial may involve a number of unsuccessful changes o
163.58: f position in the two cards, but these changes may not consume altogether more than one minute. REMARKS. As aptly described by B
163.59: inet, the operation has the following elements: "(1) To keep in mind the end to be attained, that is to say, the figure to be fo
163.60: rmed. It is necessary to comprehend this end and not to lose sight of it. (2) To try different combinations under the influence
163.61: of this directing idea, which guides the efforts of the child even though he be unconscious of the fact. (3) To judge the formed
163.62: combination, compare it with the model, and decide whether it is the correct one." It may be classed, therefore, as one of the
163.63: many forms of the "combination method." Elements must be combined into some kind of whole under the guidance of a directing idea
163.64: . In this respect it has something in common with the formboard test, the Ebbinghaus test, and the test with dissected sentences

164.1: (XII, 4). Binet designates it a "test of patience," because success in it depends upon a certain willingness to persist in a li
164.2: ne of action under the control of an idea. Not all failures in this test are equally significant. A bright child of 5 years some
164.3: times fails, but usually not without many trial combinations which he rejects one after another as unsatisfactory. A dull child
164.4: of the same age often stops after he has brought the pieces into any sort of juxtaposition, however absurd, and may be quite sat
164.5: isfied with his foolish effort. His mind is not fruitful and he lacks the power of autocriticism. It would be well worth while t
164.6: o work out a new and somewhat more difficult "test of patience," but with special care to avoid the puzzling features of the usu
164.7: al games of anagrams. The one given us by Binet is rather easy for year V, though plainly somewhat too difficult for year IV. V,
164.8: 6. THREE COMMISSIONS PROCEDURE. After getting up from the chair and moving with the child to the center of the room, say: "_Now
164.9: , I want you to do something for me. Here's a key. I want you to put it on that chair over there; then I want you to shut (or op
164.10: en) that door, and then bring me the box which you see over there_ (pointing in turn to the objects designated). _Do you underst
164.11: and? Be sure to get it right. First, put the key on the chair, then shut_ (open) _the door, then bring me the box_ (again pointi
164.12: ng). _Go ahead._" Stress the words _first_ and _then_ so as to emphasize the order in which the commissions are to be executed.
164.13: Give the commissions always in the above order. Do not repeat the instructions again or give any further aid whatever, even by t
164.14: he direction of the gaze. If the child stops or hesitates it is never permissible to say: "_What next?_" Have the selfcontrol to
164.15: leave the child alone with his task. SCORING. _All three commissions must be executed and in the proper order._ Failure may res
164.16: ult, therefore, either from leaving out one or more of the commands or from changing the order. The former is more often the cas
164.17: e. REMARKS. Success depends first on the ability to comprehend the commands, and secondly, on the ability to hold them in mind.
164.18: It is therefore a test of memory, though of a somewhat different kind from that involved in repeating digits or sentences. It is
164.19: an excellent test, for it throws light on a kind of intelligence which is demanded in all occupations and in everyday life. A m
164.20: ore difficult test of the same type ought to be worked out for a higher age level. Binet originally located this test in year VI
164.21: , but in 1911 changed it to year VII. This is unfortunate, for the three Stanford investigations, as well as the statistics of a
164.22: ll other investigators, show conclusively that it is easy enough for year V. V. ALTERNATIVE TEST: GIVING AGE PROCEDURE. The form
164.23: ula is simply, "_How old are you?_" The child of this age is, of course, not expected to know the date of his birthday, but mere
164.24: ly how many years old he is. SCORING. About the only danger in scoring is in the failure to verify the child's response. Some ch
164.25: ildren give an incorrect answer with perfect assurance, and it is therefore always necessary to verify. REMARKS. Inability to gi
164.26: ve the age may or may not be significant. If the child has arrived at the age of 7 or 8 years and has had anything like a normal
164.27: social environment, failure in the test is an extremely unfavorable sign. But if the child is an orphan or has grown up in negl
164.28: ect, ignorance of age has little significance for intelligence. About all we can say is that if a child gives his age correctly,
164.29: it is because he has had sufficient interest and intelligence to remember verbal statements which have been made concerning him
164.30: in his presence. He may even pass the test without attaching any definite meaning to the word "year." On the other hand, if he
164.31: has lived seven or eight years in a normal environment, it is safe to assume that he has heard his age given many times, and fai
164.32: lure to remember it would then indicate either a weak memory or a grave inferiority of spontaneous interests, or both. Normal ch
164.33: ildren have a natural interest in the things they hear said about themselves, while the middlegrade imbecile of even 40 years ma
164.34: y fail to remember his age, however often he may have heard it stated. Binet placed the test in year VI of the 1908 series, but
164.35: omitted it altogether in 1911. Kuhlmann and Goddard also omit it, perhaps wisely. Nevertheless, it is always interesting to give
164.36: as a supplementary test. Children from good homes acquire the knowledge about a year earlier than those from less favorable sur
164.37: roundings. Unselected children of California ordinarily pass the test at 5 years. CHAPTER XII INSTRUCTIONS FOR YEAR VI VI, 1. DI
164.38: STINGUISHING RIGHT AND LEFT PROCEDURE. Say to the child: "_Show me your right hand._" After this is responded to, say: "_Show me
164.39: your left ear._" Then: "_Show me your right eye._" Stress the words _left_ and _ear_ rather strongly and equally; also _right_
164.40: and _eye_. If there is one error, repeat the test, this time with left hand, right ear, and left eye. Carefully avoid giving any
164.41: help by look of approval or disapproval, by glancing at the part of the body indicated, or by supplementary questions. SCORING.
164.42: The test is passed if all three questions are answered correctly, or if, in case of one error, the three additional questions a
164.43: re all answered correctly. The standard, therefore, _is three out of three, or five out of six_. The chief danger of variation a
164.44: mong different examiners in scoring comes from double responses. For example, the child may point first to one ear and then to t
164.45: he other. In all cases of double response, the rule is to count the second response and disregard the first. This holds whether
164.46: the first response was wrong and the second right, or _vice versa_. REMARKS. It is interesting to follow the child's acquisition
164.47: s of language distinctions relating to spacial orientation. Other distinctions of this type are those between up and down, above
164.48: and below, near and far, before and behind, etc. As Bobertag has pointed out, the child first masters such distinctions as up a
164.49: nd down, above and below, before and behind, etc., and arrives at a knowledge of right and left rather tardily. How may we expla
164.50: in the late distinction of right and left as compared with up and down? At least four theories may be advanced: (1) Something de
164.51: pends on the frequency with which children have occasion to make the respective distinctions. (2) It may be explained on the sup
164.52: position that kinæsthetic sensations are more prominently involved in distinctions of up and down than in distinctions of right
164.53: and left. It is certainly true that, in distinguishing the two sides of a thing, less bodily movement is ordinarily required tha
164.54: n in distinctions of its upper and lower aspects. The former demands only a shift of the eyes, the latter often requires an upwa
164.55: rd or downward movement of the head. (3) It may be due to the fact that the appearance of an object is more affected by differen
164.56: ces in vertical orientation than by those of horizontal orientation. We see an object now from one side, now from the other, and
164.57: the two aspects easily blend, while the two aspects corresponding to above and below are not viewed in such rapid succession an
164.58: d so remain much more distinct from one another in the child's mind. Or, (4), the difference may be mainly a matter of language.
164.59: The child undoubtedly hears the words _up_ and _down_ much oftener than _right_ and _left_, and thus learns their meaning earli
164.60: er. Horizontal distinctions are commonly made in such terms as _this side_ and _that side_, or merely by pointing, while in the
164.61: case of vertical distinctions the words _up_ and _down_ are used constantly. This last explanation is a very plausible one, but
164.62: it is very probable that other factors are also involved. The distinction between right and left has a certain inherent and more
164.63: or less mysterious difficulty. To convince one's self of this it is only necessary to try a little experiment on the first fift
164.64: y persons one chances to meet. The experiment is as follows. Say: "I am going to ask you a question and I want you to answer it

165.1: as quickly as you can." Then ask: "Which is your right hand?" About forty persons out of fifty will answer correctly without a s
165.2: econd's hesitation, several will require two or three seconds to respond, while a few, possibly four or five per cent, will grow
165.3: confused and perhaps be unable to respond for five or ten seconds. Some very intelligent adults cannot possibly tell which is t
165.4: he right or left hand without first searching for a scar or some other distinguishing mark which is known to be on a particular
165.5: hand. Others resort to incipient movements of writing, and since, of course, every one knows which hand he writes with, the writ
165.6: ing movements automatically initiated give the desired clue. One bright little girl of 8 years responded by trying to wink first
165.7: one eye and then the other. Asked why she did this, she said she knew she could wink her left eye, but not her right! One who i
165.8: s resourceful enough to adopt such an ingenious method is surely not less intelligent than the one who is able to respond by a d
165.9: irect instead of an intermediate association. It seems that normal people never encounter a corresponding difficulty in distingu
165.10: ishing up and down. The writer has questioned several hundred without finding a single instance, whereas a great many have to em
165.11: ploy some intermediate association in order to distinguish right and left. It is the "p's and q's" that children must be told to
165.12: mind; not the "p's and b's." The former is a horizontal, the latter a vertical distinction. Considering the difficulty which no
165.13: rmal adults sometimes have in distinguishing right and left, is it fair to use this test as a measure of intelligence? We may an
165.14: swer in the affirmative. It is fair because normal adults, notwithstanding momentary uncertainty, are invariably able to make th
165.15: e distinction, if not by direct association, then by an intermediate one. We overlook the momentary confusion and regard only th
165.16: e correctness of the response. Subjects who are below middlegrade imbecile, however long they have lived, seldom pass the test.
165.17: This test found a place in year VI of Binet's 1908 scale, but was shifted to year VII in the 1911 revision. The Stanford statist
165.18: ics, and all other available data, with the exception of Bobertag's, justify its retention in year VI. It is possible that the c
165.19: hildren of different nations do not have equal opportunity and stimulus for learning the distinction between right and left, but
165.20: the data show that as far as American and English children are concerned we have a right to expect this knowledge in children o
165.21: f 6 years. VI, 2. FINDING OMISSIONS IN PICTURES PROCEDURE. Show the pictures to the child one at a time in the order in which th
165.22: ey are lettered, _a_, _b_, _c_, _d_. When the first picture is shown (that with the eye lacking), say: "_There is something wron
165.23: g with this face. It is not all there. Part of it is left out. Look carefully and tell me what part of the face is not there._"
165.24: Often the child gives an irrelevant answer; as, "The feet are gone," "The stomach is not there," etc. These statements are true,
165.25: but they do not satisfy the requirements of the test, so we say: "_No; I am talking about the face. Look again and tell me what
165.26: is left out of the face._" If the correct response does not follow, we point to the place where the eye should be and say: "_Se
165.27: e, the eye is gone._" When picture _b_ is shown we say merely: "_What is left out of this face?_" Likewise with picture _c_. For
165.28: picture _d_ we say: "_What is left out of this picture?_" No help of any kind is given unless (if necessary) with the first pic
165.29: ture. With the others we confine ourselves to the single question, and the answer should be given promptly, say within twenty to
165.30: twentyfive seconds. SCORING. Passed if the omission is correctly pointed out in _three out of four_ of the pictures. Certain mi
165.31: nor errors we may overlook, such as "eyes" instead of "eye" for the first picture; "nose and one ear" instead of merely "nose" f
165.32: or the third; "hands" instead of "arms" for the fourth, etc. Errors like the following, however, count as failure: "The other ey
165.33: e," or "The other ear" for the first or third; "The ears" for the fourth, etc. REMARKS. The test is one of the two or three doze
165.34: n forms of the socalled "completion test," all of which have it in common that from the given parts of a whole the missing parts
165.35: are to be found. The whole to be completed may be a word, a sentence, a story, a picture, a group of pictures, an object, or in
165.36: fact almost anything. Sometimes all the parts of the whole are given and only the arrangement or order is to be found, as in th
165.37: e test with dissected sentences. Further discussion of the completion test will be found in connection with test 4, year XII. Fo
165.38: r the present we will only observe that notwithstanding a certain similarity among the tests of this type, they do not all call
165.39: into play the same mental processes. The factor most involved may be verbal language coherence, visual perception of form, the a
165.40: ssociation of abstract ideas, etc. To pass Binet's test with mutilated pictures requires, (1) that the parts of the picture be p
165.41: erceived as constituting a whole; and (2) that the idea of a human face or form be so easily and so clearly reproducible that it
165.42: may act, even before it comes fully into consciousness, as a model or pattern, for the criticism of the picture shown. The youn
165.43: ger the child, the less adequate, in this sense, is his perceptual familiarity with common objects. In standardizing a series of
165.44: "absurd pictures," the writer has found that normal children of 3 years often see nothing wrong in a picture which shows a cat
165.45: with two legs or a hen with four legs. Such children would, of course, never mistake a cat for a hen. Their trouble lies in the
165.46: inability to call up in clear form a "free idea" of a cat or a hen for comparison with the perceptual presentation offered by th
165.47: e picture. Middlegrade imbeciles of adult age have much the same difficulty as normal children of 4 years in recognizing mutilat
165.48: ions or absurdities in pictures of familiar objects. Binet first placed this test in year VII, changing it to year VIII in the 1
165.49: 911 revision. In other revisions it has been retained in year VII, although all the available statistics except Bobertag's warra
165.50: nt its location in year VI. VI, 3. COUNTING THIRTEEN PENNIES PROCEDURE. The procedure is the same as in the test of counting fou
165.51: r pennies (year IV, test 3). If the first response contains only a minor error, such as the omission of a number in counting, fa
165.52: ilure to tally with the finger, etc., a second trial is given. SCORING. The test is passed if there is _one success in two trial
165.53: s_. Success requires that the counting should tally with the pointing. It is not sufficient merely to state the number of pennie
165.54: s without pointing, for unless the child points and counts aloud we cannot be sure that his correct answer may not be the joint
165.55: result of two errors in opposite directions and equal; for example, if one penny were skipped and another were counted twice the
165.56: total result would still be correct, but the performance would not satisfy the requirements. REMARKS. Does success in this test
165.57: depend upon intelligence or upon schooling? The answer is, intelligence mainly. There are possibly a few normal 6yearold childr
165.58: en who could not pass the test for lack of instruction, but children of this age usually have enough spontaneous interest in num
165.59: bers to acquire facility in counting as far as 13 without formal teaching. Certainly, inability to do so by the age of 7 years i
165.60: s a suspicious sign unless the child's environment has been extraordinarily unfavorable. On the other hand, feebleminded adults
165.61: of the 5year level usually have to have a great deal of instruction before they acquire the ability to count 13, and many of the
165.62: m are hardly able to learn it at all. So much does our learning depend on original endowment. Binet originally placed this test
165.63: in year VII, but moved it to year VI in 1911. All the statistics, without exception, show that this change was justified. Bobert
165.64: ag says that nearly all 7yearolds who are not feebleminded can pass it, a statement with which we can fully agree. VI, 4. COMPRE

166.1: HENSION, SECOND DEGREE PROCEDURE. The questions used in this year are: (a) "_What's the thing to do if it is raining when you st
166.2: art to school?_" (b) "_What's the thing to do if you find that your house is on fire?_" (c) "_What's the thing to do if you are
166.3: going some place and miss your train (car)?_" Note that the wording of the first part of the questions is slightly different fro
166.4: m that in year IV, test 5. If there is no response, or if the child looks puzzled, the question may be repeated once or twice. T
166.5: he form of the question must not under any circumstances be altered. Question _b_, for example, would be materially changed if w
166.6: e should say: "_Suppose you were to come home from school and find that your house was burning up. What would you do?_" The expr
166.7: ession "burning up" would probably be much less likely to suggest calling a fireman than would the words "on fire." SCORING. _Tw
166.8: o out of three_ must be answered correctly. The harder the comprehension questions are, the greater the variety of answers and t
166.9: he greater the difficulty of scoring. Because of the difficulty many examiners find in scoring this test, we will list the most
166.10: common satisfactory, unsatisfactory, and doubtful responses to each question. (a) _If it is raining when you start to school_ _S
166.11: atisfactory._ "Take umbrella," "Bring a parasol," "Put on rubbers," "Wear an overcoat," etc. This type of response occurred 61 t
166.12: imes out of 72 successes. "Have my father bring me" also counts _plus_. _Unsatisfactory._ "Go home," "Stay at home," "Stay in th
166.13: e house," "Have the rainbow," "Stay in school," etc. "Stay at home" is the most common failure and might at first seem to the ex
166.14: aminer to be a satisfactory response. As a matter of fact, this answer rests on a slight misunderstanding of the question, the i
166.15: mport of which is that one is to go to school and it is raining. _Doubtful._ "Run" as an answer is a little more troublesome. It
166.16: may reasonably be scored _plus_ if it can be ascertained that the child is accustomed to meet the situation in this way. It is
166.17: a common response with children in those regions of the Southwest where rains are so infrequent that umbrellas are rarely used.
166.18: "Bring my lunch" may be considered a satisfactory response in case the child is in the habit of so doing on rainy days. (b) _If
166.19: you find that your house is on fire_ _Satisfactory._ "Ring the fire alarm," "Call the firemen," "Call for help," "Put water on i
166.20: t," etc. _Unsatisfactory._ The most common failure, accounting for nearly half of all, is to suggest finding other shelter; _e.g
166.21: ._, "Go to the hotel," "Get another house," "Stay with your friends," "Build a new house," etc. Others are: "Tell them you are s
166.22: orry it burned down," "Be careful and not let it burn again," "Have it insured," "Cry," "Call the policeman," etc. _Doubtful._ I
166.23: nstead of suggesting measures to put out the fire, a good many children suggest mere escape or the saving of household articles.
166.24: Responses of this type are: "Jump out of the windows," "Save yourself," "Get out as fast as you can," "Save the baby," "Get my
166.25: dolls and jewelry and hurry and get out." These answers are about one seventh as frequent as the perfectly satisfactory ones, an
166.26: d the rule for scoring them is a matter of some importance. Under certain circumstances the logical thing to do would be to save
166.27: one's self or valuables without wasting time trying to call help. There may be no help in reach, or a fire which the child imag
166.28: ines may be too far along for help to be effective. In order to avoid the possibility of doing a subject an injustice, it may be
166.29: desirable to score such answers _plus_. We must not be too arbitrary. (c) _If you miss your train_ _Satisfactory._ The answer w
166.30: e expect is, "Wait for another," "Take the next car," or something to that effect. This type of answer includes about 85 per cen
166.31: t of the responses which do not belong obviously in the unsatisfactory group. "Take a jitney" is a modern variation of this resp
166.32: onse which must be counted as satisfactory. _Unsatisfactory._ These are endless. One continues to meet new examples of absurdity
166.33: , however many children one has tested. The possibilities are literally inexhaustible, but the following are among the most comm
166.34: on: "Wait for it to come back," "Have to walk," "Be mad," "Don't swear," "Run and try to catch it," "Try to jump on," "Don't go
166.35: to that place," "Go to the next station," etc. _Doubtful._ The main doubtful response is, "Go home again," "Come back next day a
166.36: nd catch another," etc. In small or isolated towns having only one or two trains per day, this is the logical thing to do, and i
166.37: n such cases the score is _plus_. Fortunately, only about one answer in ten gives rise to any difference of opinion among even p
166.38: artly trained examiners. REMARKS. The three comprehension questions of this group were all suggested by Binet in 1905. Only one

168.42: elf well to exact quantitative standardization. Its value has been questioned, however, on two grounds: (1) That it is not a tes

168.44: ery. As to the first objection, it is true that more than one mental function is brought into play by the test. The same may be
168.45: said of every other test in the Binet scale and for that matter of any test that could be devised. It is impossible to isolate a
168.46: ny function for separate testing. In fact, the functions called memory, attention, perception, judgment, etc., never operate in

168.48: acterizing mental processes of various types. In any test it is "general ability" which is operative, perhaps now _chiefly_ in r
168.49: emembering, at another time _chiefly_ in sensory discrimination, again in reasoning, etc. The second objection, that the test is
168.50: largely invalidated by the existence of imagery types, is not borne out by the facts. Experiments have shown that pure imagery

185.51: ally rather intelligent ones, hit upon the device of counting or putting words together in sentences. We then break in with: "_C

185.61: , have various parts, different uses and accessories, and that in enumerating all these they could find a large number of words.

194.1: d the paper, hold it up before the subject so as to let him see the result. The answer is often incorrect and the unfolded sheet

194.5: holes._" At this point fold the paper a third time and say: "_Now, I am folding it again. How many holes will it have this time
194.6: when I unfold it?_" Record the answer and again unfold the paper while the subject looks on. Continue in the same manner with sh

194.9: n we folded it again there were four, when we folded it again there were eight, when we folded it again there were sixteen; now,

194.11: once, twice, three times_," etc., as this often leads the subject to double the numeral heard instead of doubling the number of
194.12: holes in the previously folded sheet. After the answer is given, do not fail to unfold the paper and let the subject view the re
